m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Check that your computer, browser, and speakers are ready for class.
  • Open the Scratch editor in the way that fits your home: no account, an account, or the app.
  • Pick a safe username with a grown-up, if you make an account.
  • Run a three-block test and know for sure that it worked.

Here's your goal for today, and it takes about ten minutes. You click a little green flag, an orange cat on your screen says "Hello!", and then it meows. That's it. If you can make that happen, your computer is ready for six weeks of games and animations.

Scratch is a free coding tool created at the MIT Media Lab and run today by the Scratch Foundation, a nonprofit. Instead of typing code, you snap colored blocks together, a bit like LEGO bricks that give orders. You can't break your computer with it, and nothing in this class costs money.

#What you need

You need Why it matters
A laptop or desktop (Windows, Mac, or Chromebook) Dragging blocks is easiest on a big screen.
An up-to-date web browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari Scratch runs inside the browser, so an old browser is the most common reason it won't load.
Internet For the live class call and for the online editor.
A mouse (nice to have) A trackpad works, but it's easy to drop a block in the wrong spot.
Headphones (nice to have) Your projects will meow, beep, and play music. Headphones keep that out of the class call.

A tablet can run the online editor, but our games in Weeks 2 and 3 use the arrow keys, so a keyboard helps a lot. Phones are too small for the editor.

#Pick how you'll open Scratch

There are three ways in. All three give you the same Scratch 3 editor with the same blocks, so you won't miss anything whichever you choose. The only real difference is where your projects get saved.

Option Where your work is saved Needs internet?
A: online, no account Only where you save it yourself, as a file Yes
B: online, with account Online, in your account, from any computer Yes
C: the Scratch app As a file on your computer No

#Option A: the online editor, no account

This is the fastest way to start, and it's what most students use on the first day.

  1. Open your browser.
  2. Type scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor into the address bar and press Enter.
  3. You'll know it worked when you see an orange cat standing in a white rectangle on the right, and a column of colored circles down the left side.

Bookmark that page so you can get back in one click.

The catch: without an account, Scratch forgets your project the moment you close the tab. You'll save your work as a file on your computer. The lesson after next shows exactly how.

#Option B: the online editor, with an account

A free account saves your projects online, so you can open them from home, school, or a friend's house. It also lets you share projects with the Scratch community later in the course.

⚠️ Watch out

Make your account with a parent or guardian, not on your own. Scratch asks for an email address. For kids, that's a grown-up's email, and Scratch sends that grown-up a link to confirm the account. In some places a parent has to give permission before the account works at all.

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu and click Join Scratch at the top.
  2. Make a username. Scratch asks you not to use any part of your real name, and that's good advice: your username shows up on everything you share. "PixelTiger42" is great. "MayaJohnson2015" tells strangers your name and your age.
  3. Make a password. Keep it secret from everyone except your grown-up.
  4. Answer the next questions together, such as your country and the month and year you were born. Scratch doesn't show these on your profile.
  5. Enter your grown-up's email address. They open the email from Scratch and click the link inside.
  6. Back on the site, click Create at the top to open the editor.

When you're signed in, your username appears in the top-right corner of the editor. That's how you know your work is being saved to your account.

#Option C: the Scratch app (works offline)

If your internet is slow or keeps dropping, install the app. Go to scratch.mit.edu/download first, then follow the steps for your computer:

Windows

  1. On the download page, choose Windows.
  2. Click the Microsoft Store link, then click Get or Install in the Store. (If the page also offers a direct download, running that .exe file works too.)
  3. Open Scratch 3 from the Start menu.

macOS

  1. On the download page, choose macOS.
  2. Get it from the Mac App Store, or use the direct download: open the .dmg file and drag Scratch 3 into your Applications folder.
  3. Open Scratch from Launchpad or the Applications folder.

Chromebook

  1. On the download page, choose ChromeOS and follow the link to the Google Play Store.
  2. Install the app and open it from your launcher.
  3. School Chromebooks often block new apps. If yours does, use Option A instead; it works on every Chromebook.

The app doesn't sign in to a Scratch account, so you'll save projects as files. On a Chromebook the app keeps projects inside itself, and you get a file out through the three-dot menu on a project.

💡 Tip

Can't decide? Start with Option A today. You can make an account later with your grown-up, and every file you saved will still open in it.

#The three-block test

Time to prove it all works. You'll build a script that is exactly three blocks long. A script is a stack of blocks that runs from top to bottom.

  1. On the far left, click the yellow Events circle. Drag when green flag clicked into the big empty area in the middle.
  2. Click the purple Looks circle. Drag say [Hello!] for (2) seconds and drop it just under the first block. When it's close, a gray shadow shows where it will land. Let go and it clicks into place.
  3. Click the pink Sound circle. Snap play sound (Meow v) until done under that.

Your script should look like this:

Now click the green flag above the stage (the white area where the cat lives). A speech bubble saying "Hello!" pops up over the cat. Two seconds later it disappears, and you hear a meow.

Bubble and meow? You're ready for Week 1.

🧪 Try it yourself

Click inside the white bubble of the say block, type your own name instead of "Hello!", and click the flag again. Then change the 2 to 5. Notice the meow waits until the bubble is gone.

#When the test doesn't work

These are the problems students really hit on day one, with the fix for each.

#Nothing happens when I click the flag

Look closely at your blocks. If there's a gap between two of them, they aren't connected, and a loose block never runs. Drag the lower block up until it clicks. Also check that when green flag clicked is at the top of the stack. That yellow block with the rounded top is what listens for the flag.

#I see the bubble but hear no meow

Turn up your computer's volume. Then look at the browser tab for a speaker icon with a line through it: that means the tab is muted, and clicking the icon unmutes it. If you use headphones, check they're plugged in all the way.

#The page is blank, gray, or never finishes loading

Update your browser, or try a different one. Very old browsers like Internet Explorer can't run Scratch 3 at all. On a school computer, the network might block Scratch; ask your teacher, or use the app at home.

#The website keeps asking me to sign in

You never have to sign in to use the editor. Go straight to scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor instead of the home page.

#My blocks keep landing in the wrong place

That's almost always a trackpad. Plug in a mouse if you have one. If not, press and hold firmly, drag slowly, and watch for the gray shadow before you let go.

#Staying safe on Scratch

Scratch has millions of users, many of them kids, and it has rules called the Community Guidelines to keep it friendly. The most important one for you: never put your full name, address, school, phone number, or passwords in a project, a comment, or your profile. If something online makes you uncomfortable, stop, and tell a grown-up or your teacher. Every project and comment on Scratch also has a Report button.

#Further reading

  • Download the Scratch app (opens in a new tab): the official install steps and FAQ for each kind of computer.
  • Scratch for parents (opens in a new tab): what Scratch is and how accounts work, written for grown-ups. Good to read together.
  • Scratch Community Guidelines (opens in a new tab): the short list of rules everyone on Scratch agrees to.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Name the five areas of the Scratch editor and say what each one is for.
  • Find a block by its color and drag it into a script.
  • Build, run, and fix a short project called "Meet Me".
  • Check that your project starts the same way every time you click the flag.

Twenty minutes from now, this is what you'll have. You click the green flag. The cat jumps to the left edge of the stage, slides into the middle, and says "Hi! I'm Sam." Then it tells everyone something you love, flips upside down, flips back, and meows. Your own name and your own facts go in, of course.

Here's the whole thing. It's eight blocks:

Don't worry if it looks like a lot. By the end of the tour you'll know where every one of those blocks lives.

#The five areas of the editor

Open the editor (scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor, or the Scratch app). Your screen splits into five areas. Here's how they work together:

#1. The block palette (left)

Down the far left is a column of colored circles. Each one is a category of blocks: Motion (blue), Looks (purple), Sound (pink), Events (yellow), Control (orange), Sensing (light blue), Operators (green), Variables (dark orange), and My Blocks (red). Click a circle and the list jumps to those blocks.

The colors are your map. If you see a purple block in someone's project, you know to look for it in Looks.

#2. The code area (middle)

The big empty space. You drag blocks here and snap them into scripts. You can have lots of scripts in one code area, each one sitting on its own.

#3. The stage (top right)

The white rectangle where your project plays. Above it sit the green flag (start) and the red stop sign (stop everything). Small buttons in the top-right corner switch between a small stage, a normal stage, and full screen.

#4. The sprite pane (bottom right)

Every character or object in a project is a sprite. The cat is a sprite called Sprite1. This pane lists all your sprites, and the boxes above them show the selected sprite's name, its position (x and y), whether it's showing, its size, and its direction. The cat-face button in the corner adds a new sprite.

#5. The Stage button and the three tabs

To the right of the sprite pane is the Stage button, where you choose a backdrop, the picture behind everything. At the top left of the editor are three tabs: Code, Costumes, and Sounds. They always show the code, pictures, or sounds of whatever is selected right now.

💡 Tip

Code belongs to the sprite that's highlighted in the sprite pane. If your blocks suddenly "vanished," you probably clicked a different sprite or the Stage. Click the cat again and your code is back.

#Build "Meet Me", one step at a time

Each step adds a few blocks, then you click the green flag to see what changed. Testing after every step is a habit real programmers have: when something breaks, you know it was the last thing you added.

#Step 1: Start with a hat block

Every script needs a hat block on top. It has a rounded top, and it decides when the script runs. From Events, drag out when green flag clicked.

#Step 2: Put the cat on its starting mark

From Motion, snap go to x: () y: () under the hat. Click each white bubble and type a number: -150 for x and 0 for y.

Click the green flag. The cat jumps to the left side of the stage. Drag the cat somewhere else and click the flag again: it jumps right back. Next week you'll learn what x and y really mean. For now, -150 is "over on the left."

#Step 3: Slide in and say hello

Add glide (1) secs to x: () y: () from Motion, then two say [] for () seconds blocks from Looks. Change the glide time to 2, and type your own words in the bubbles.

Click the flag. The cat jumps left, slides to the middle over two seconds, then shows each bubble for two seconds.

#Step 4: Flip and meow

From Motion, add turn right (15) degrees (in the editor it shows a curved arrow instead of the word "right"). Change 15 to 180. Then add a wait (1) seconds from Control, set it to 0.5, and add a second turn. Finish with play sound (Meow v) until done from Sound.

Why the wait? Scratch is fast. Two turns in a row, with nothing between them, both happen before the screen even redraws, so you'd never see the cat flip. The half-second wait lets you see it upside down before it turns back. Two half-turns of 180 degrees make one full circle, so the cat ends facing the way it started.

#Step 5: Pick a backdrop

Hover over the Choose a Backdrop button (bottom right, under the Stage button) and click it. Pick any picture you like. Then click the cat in the sprite pane so your code shows again.

#Step 6: Name your project

Signed in to an account? Click the title box at the top of the editor (it says Untitled) and type Meet Me. No account? You'll give the project its name when you save it as a file in the next lesson.

🧪 Try it yourself

Make the cat introduce you with three facts instead of two. Then try changing the glide time from 2 to 0.5. Does it look like the cat is sneaking or sprinting?

#Proof it works

Click the green flag twice in a row and check every box both times:

  • The cat starts on the left every time, even if you dragged it away.
  • It glides to the middle.
  • Both speech bubbles show your words.
  • It flips upside down, flips back, and meows.
  • There's a backdrop behind it.

All five, twice? Your Scratch setup works. Save it right now: File > Save to your computer, or File > Save now if you have an account.

#What usually goes wrong

  • The glide doesn't go where you expect. There are two glide blocks in Motion. You may have grabbed glide (1) secs to (random position v). Swap it for the one with x and y.
  • The cat stays upside down. You have only one turn right (180) degrees. Add the second one after the wait.
  • The cat never flips at all. The wait is missing between the two turns.
  • The cat runs off somewhere strange. Check the minus sign. -150 is the left side and 150 is the right.
  • A block won't snap. Drag it by its left edge and drop it so its top lines up just under the block above.
  • I clicked a block in the palette and the cat moved. That's not a bug. Clicking any block runs it once, which is a handy way to test one block by itself.

Predict before you click

2 questions

1You delete the go to x: (-150) y: (0) block, then click the green flag twice. Where does the cat start the second run?

  • Nothing sends it there anymore. That was the job of the block you deleted.

  • Scratch remembers where a sprite ended. Without a starting block, the second run begins wherever the first one finished.

  • The script still runs. Only the starting position is missing.

Show answer

B. Scratch remembers where a sprite ended. Without a starting block, the second run begins wherever the first one finished.

2You move the play sound (Meow v) until done block so it sits right under the hat block, above everything else. What do you notice?

  • "Until done" means the script waits for the sound to finish before running the next block.

  • That's what a sound block without "until done" would do. This one makes the rest of the script wait.

  • The sound still plays. Blocks run top to bottom, so it just plays earlier.

Show answer

A. "Until done" means the script waits for the sound to finish before running the next block.

  • Getting Started tutorial (opens in a new tab): the official step-by-step tutorial that opens right inside the editor, with short videos for each step.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Know what happens before, during, and after each live class.
  • Save a project as an .sb3 file and open it again, or use Save now with an account.
  • Keep every week's project in one folder with a name you'll recognize.
  • Fix the most common "it's not working" problems by yourself, and ask for help in a way that gets a fast answer.

Picture this. You spend a whole class building a bouncing-ball game. It's great. Then you close the browser tab to go eat dinner, and when you come back, the editor shows a plain orange cat and nothing else. Without an account, the online editor doesn't keep your work for you, so the game is gone.

This happens to almost everyone once. After this lesson, it won't happen to you.

#What a class week looks like

We meet live online once a week for an hour and a half, six weeks in a row. Every week in this course has the same three parts:

  1. Notes. Your teacher explains the week's new blocks with small examples. Come back and reread them whenever something didn't stick.
  2. Code-along. We build one project together, step by step, and you build it in your own editor at the same time. Falling behind is normal. Say so in the chat, and your teacher will slow down.
  3. Practice. Challenges to try on your own, from easy to tricky. Each one has a hint and a solution. Try first, then peek at the hint, and only then open the solution. Skipping straight to the answer is like reading the last page of a mystery.

#Before each class

  • Open the Scratch editor and click the green flag on anything, just to be sure it works.
  • Have last week's project ready, either as a file or in your account.
  • Put on headphones if you have them, so project sounds don't mix with the call.

#During class

  • Keep the class call in one window and Scratch in another. With one screen, switch back and forth.
  • Ask questions any time. "My cat disappeared" is a perfectly good question, and other people usually have the same one.

#Saving without an account

Without an account, saving means downloading your project as a file that ends in .sb3. That's Scratch's file type, like .docx for a Word document.

  1. Click File at the top left of the editor.
  2. Click Save to your computer.
  3. Depending on your browser, the file goes straight into your Downloads folder, or a box pops up asking where to save it and what to call it. If it asks, choose your class folder (see below) and type a good name.

At first the file is usually called Scratch Project.sb3. Give it a name you'll recognize, like week1-meet-me.sb3, and always keep .sb3 at the end. Here's how to find and rename it on your computer:

Windows

  1. Open File Explorer (the folder icon on the taskbar) and click Downloads on the left.
  2. Right-click Scratch Project.sb3 and choose Rename.
  3. Type the new name, keep the .sb3 ending, and press Enter.

macOS

  1. Open Finder and click Downloads in the sidebar.
  2. Click the file once, then press Return to edit its name.
  3. Type the new name, keep the .sb3 ending, and press Return again.

Chromebook

  1. Open the Files app and click Downloads under My files.
  2. Right-click the file and choose Rename.
  3. Type the new name, keep the .sb3 ending, and press Enter.

⚠️ Watch out

Each time you click Save to your computer, you make a brand-new copy of the file. It doesn't update the old one. Save after every big change and always at the end of class, use names with the week in them (week2-dance.sb3), and delete old copies you don't need.

#Opening your file again

  1. Open the editor.
  2. Click File > Load from your computer.
  3. Find your .sb3 file and open it.

Scratch may ask whether to replace the project that's on screen. Say yes only if you've already saved whatever you were working on, because the old one will be swapped out.

#Saving with an account

When you're signed in, your projects are saved online.

  • Scratch saves by itself every so often while you work. Click File > Save now whenever you want to be sure.
  • Type a name in the title box at the top (instead of Untitled) so you can find the project later.
  • File > Save as a copy makes a second version. Use it before you try a wild idea, so the original stays safe.

To find your projects again, click the folder icon in the top bar. That page is called My Stuff, and it lists every project you've made, newest first. Click See inside to open one in the editor.

Your projects stay private until you click Share. We'll talk about sharing safely near the end of the course.

#Keep everything in one folder

Make a folder on your computer called Scratch Class, and put every project in it, named by week:

Even with an account, downloading a copy at the end of each class is a smart backup. Websites go down sometimes; a file on your computer doesn't.

#Getting unstuck

When a project misbehaves, run through these questions in order. Most problems are solved by the first three.

#My sprite disappeared

It may have walked off the edge, shrunk to nothing, or been hidden by a hide block. Click the sprite in the sprite pane and look at its boxes: is Show turned off? Is the size tiny? A reset script at the start of every project fixes all of it at once:

Click the green flag and the sprite appears in the exact middle of the stage, facing right, at normal size, with its normal colors.

#I deleted my sprite by mistake

Click Edit > Restore Sprite right away. It brings back the last sprite you deleted, code and all.

#I deleted some blocks by mistake

Right-click an empty part of the code area and choose Undo. Pressing Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) right after clicking the code area works too.

#My code is a messy pile

Right-click an empty spot in the code area and choose Clean up Blocks. Scratch lines up all your scripts in a neat column.

#There's no sound

Check your computer's volume, look for a muted speaker icon on the browser tab, and make sure your headphones are plugged in all the way.

#Load from your computer can't find my file

Look in your Downloads folder first. If the file's name ends in something like .sb3.txt, rename it so it ends in .sb3 again.

#Scratch is really slow

Close other tabs and programs. If it's still slow, try a different browser, or install the Scratch app.

#How to ask for help so you get a fast answer

"It doesn't work" is hard for anyone to fix. Try this instead: say what you expected, what happened instead, and what you already tried.

A teacher can usually spot the problem from those three lines, often before you even share your screen.

#Your setup checklist

Before Week 1, make sure you can do all four:

  • Open the editor.
  • Run a script with the green flag.
  • Save a project, either to your computer or with Save now.
  • Close the editor, open it again, and get your project back.

If you can do all four, you're ready for the first class.

#Further reading

  • My Stuff on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): everything the My Stuff page can do once you have an account.
  • Project File on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): what's inside an .sb3 file, if you're curious.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what a sprite is, and what the stage is.
  • Find any spot on the stage using its x and y numbers.
  • Choose between go to, glide, change x by, and move for the motion you want.
  • Animate a sprite by switching costumes, and change the scene with backdrops.
  • Reset size, effects, and position at the start of a script so it runs the same every time.

Ask a friend to stand "over there" and they'll say "where?" A computer can't even ask. It needs an exact address. In Scratch, every spot on the stage has an address made of two numbers, and once you can read them, you can send a sprite anywhere.

Here's a script that walks the cat around the whole stage in a rectangle. By the end of this page, every number in it will make sense to you:

#Sprites act, the stage holds the scene

A sprite is anything that can move or do things: a character, a ball, a button, a cloud. Each sprite has its own scripts, its own costumes (pictures), and its own sounds. When you click a sprite in the sprite pane, you see its code.

The stage is the background that all the sprites stand on. It can have scripts too, but it can't move around. Instead of costumes it has backdrops.

To add a sprite, hover over the cat-face button at the bottom of the sprite pane:

  • Choose a Sprite opens the library, full of ready-made characters and objects.
  • Paint opens a blank costume so you can draw your own.
  • Surprise picks a random sprite for you.
  • Upload Sprite adds a picture from your computer.

#The stage is a map with x and y

The stage is 480 steps wide and 360 steps tall. Every spot on it has two numbers:

  • x tells you how far left or right. The left edge is -240, the middle is 0, and the right edge is 240.
  • y tells you how far up or down. The bottom edge is -180, the middle is 0, and the top edge is 180.

People write a spot as (x, y), x first. So (120, 90) means 120 to the right of the middle and 90 up. Two tricks for remembering which is which: x goes across (say "x is a cross"), and y reaches up to the sky. And whenever you see a minus sign, think "left" for x or "down" for y.

You don't have to guess the numbers. Drag a sprite around the stage and watch the x and y boxes in the sprite pane change as it moves. Want to see them on the stage itself? In Motion, tick the checkboxes next to x position and y position at the bottom of the list.

🧪 Try it yourself

Before you drag anything, guess: where is (0, 180)? Where is (-240, -180)? Now drag the cat to each spot and read the boxes. (The cat can't go exactly to an edge, because Scratch keeps part of every sprite on the stage, but you'll get close.)

#Four ways to move

Motion blocks are blue. These are the ones you'll use the most:

Block What it does
go to x: (0) y: (0) Jumps to a spot instantly, like teleporting
glide (1) secs to x: (0) y: (0) Slides to a spot, taking that many seconds
change x by (10) Shifts right (or left, with a negative number)
change y by (10) Shifts up (or down, with a negative number)
set x to (0) Jumps sideways to that x and keeps the same y
move (10) steps Walks forward in whatever direction the sprite is facing
turn right (15) degrees Spins clockwise
point in direction (90) Faces a direction

Now look at the rectangle script at the top again. It starts with go to, which plants the cat in the bottom-left corner at (-200, -120). Each glide then slides it to the next corner: across to the right (x changes, y stays), up (y changes), back to the left, and down to where it started. Four glides of one second each, so the trip takes four seconds.

#Teleport or walk?

go to is a teleport: no time passes, and you never see the trip. glide is a walk: you watch the sprite travel. Use go to to put a sprite on its starting mark, and glide when the movement is part of the show.

#Directions and move

move (10) steps doesn't know about left or right. It walks forward, wherever the sprite is facing. Directions in Scratch are measured like a compass, in degrees:

Direction Faces
90 right (every new sprite starts here)
-90 left
0 up
180 down

So point in direction (-90) followed by move (50) steps sends the cat 50 steps to the left. change x by (-50) gets it to the same spot without turning at all.

#Why so many scripts start with go to

Scratch remembers where a sprite was when the last run ended. Suppose your script only says change x by (50). The first click moves the cat 50 steps right. The second click moves it 50 more, then 50 more, until it's squashed against the right edge. Putting go to x: () y: () at the top sends it back to the starting line every single time.

#Costumes: a sprite's flipbook

A costume is one picture of a sprite. The cat comes with two, called costume1 and costume2, and its legs are in different places in each. Flip between them quickly and the cat looks like it's walking, just like the drawings in the corner of a flipbook.

Open the Costumes tab to see them. You can paint on them, recolor them, or add new ones. Here's a three-step walk:

The cat steps right three times and its legs change between each step. The wait (0.3) seconds blocks come from Control, and they matter more than they look. Scratch runs blocks so fast that, without waits, every costume change would happen before the screen redraws, and you'd see the cat jump to the end with no walking at all.

Next week, loops will repeat this for us so we don't have to stack the same blocks again and again.

#Backdrops change the scene

A backdrop is like a costume for the stage. Click Choose a Backdrop at the bottom right of the editor to add one. Any sprite can switch the backdrop, which is how a story moves from one scene to the next:

If your project has a second backdrop, the scene changes right after the cat finishes talking. With only one backdrop, nothing seems to happen, so add another before you test it.

#Looks blocks change how a sprite appears

Looks blocks are purple. Here are the ones you'll reach for most:

  • say [Hi!] for (2) seconds and think [Hmm...] for (2) seconds show speech and thought bubbles.
  • change size by (10) and set size to (100) % make a sprite grow or shrink.
  • change [color v] effect by (25) tints the sprite. Click the dropdown for other effects: ghost (see-through), brightness, fisheye, whirl, pixelate, and mosaic.
  • clear graphic effects turns every effect off.
  • show and hide make a sprite appear and disappear.
  • go to [front v] layer puts a sprite in front of all the others.

A thought bubble appears, then the cat grows to 150% and turns green, then it talks. Now look at the first two blocks under the hat. Sizes and effects stay after a project stops, so without those two reset blocks the cat would be 200% and a new color on the second run, 250% on the third, and so on.

#What usually goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

Mixing up x and y. If your sprite goes up when you wanted it to go right, you changed y instead of x. Say it out loud: "x is across, y is up."

  • Forgetting the minus sign. change x by (-10) goes left. change x by (10) goes right.
  • Effects that pile up. Size and effects survive between runs. Reset them at the top of your script.
  • move going the "wrong" way. move follows the sprite's direction. If the cat is facing left, move (10) steps goes left.
  • Editing the wrong sprite. The Costumes tab only shows the selected sprite's costumes. Check which sprite is highlighted.

#Check yourself

Each script below starts with the cat in the middle, at (0, 0), facing right at size 100%. Predict, then answer.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Where does the cat end up after Script A?

  • change x by (100) moves it right to x = 100, then change y by (-50) moves it down to y = -50.

  • That swaps x and y. The first change is to x, the second is to y.

  • The minus sign on -50 means down, so y becomes negative.

  • The go to only sets the start. The two change blocks still move it.

Show answer

A. change x by (100) moves it right to x = 100, then change y by (-50) moves it down to y = -50.

2Where does the cat end up after Script B?

  • That's where it would go facing right. point in direction (-90) turned it to face left first.

  • move walks forward in the direction the sprite faces. It's facing left, so 50 steps takes x from 0 to -50.

  • Direction -90 is left, not down. Down is 180.

Show answer

B. move walks forward in the direction the sprite faces. It's facing left, so 50 steps takes x from 0 to -50.

3You click the green flag on Script C three times. How big is the cat now?

  • That would be true if the size reset each time, but nothing in this script resets it.

  • Size stays between runs: 100 becomes 120, then 140, then 160. Adding set size to (100) % at the top would fix it.

  • change size by (20) really does change the size, and it isn't undone when the project stops.

Show answer

B. Size stays between runs: 100 becomes 120, then 140, then 160. Adding set size to (100) % at the top would fix it.

4You want the cat to slowly drift across the stage so the audience watches it travel. Which block fits best?

  • go to teleports. The cat would just appear at the end.

  • glide shows the whole trip, and the number of seconds sets how slow it looks.

  • Like go to, this jumps instantly.

Show answer

B. glide shows the whole trip, and the number of seconds sets how slow it looks.

Key takeaways

  • The stage is 480 by 360. The middle is (0, 0), x runs from -240 to 240, and y runs from -180 to 180.
  • go to teleports, glide shows the trip, and change x by and change y by shift a sprite without turning it.
  • move walks in whatever direction the sprite faces: 90 is right, -90 left, 0 up, 180 down.
  • Costumes are a sprite's flipbook. A wait between costume changes makes the animation visible.
  • Position, size, and effects stay after a run ends, so start scripts with reset blocks.

What you'll learn

  • Plan a short story as scenes before you build it.
  • Use a reset script so the story starts the same way every time.
  • Combine move, next costume, and wait to make a walk.
  • Use hide, show, size, and the ghost effect to make a sprite look far away.
  • Change scenes with switch backdrop to.

Our cat has a dream: it wants to go to space. By the end of class it will get there, in a short animated movie with two scenes. Here's the plan, scene by scene:

When it's done, clicking the green flag plays the whole movie in about 15 seconds: the cat walks into a sunny park, wonders about the stars, counts down, and rockets out of the top of the stage. The scene switches to a starry sky, and the cat drifts up from below, tiny and see-through like it's far away, does a slow spin, and glows a new color.

Everything in it comes from this week's Notes: x and y, gliding, costumes, backdrops, and Looks effects.

#Step 1: Set up both scenes

Start a new project with File > New.

  1. Click Choose a Backdrop (bottom right).
  2. Type Blue Sky in the search box and click it.
  3. Click Choose a Backdrop again and pick Stars.

Your stage now has three backdrops: the plain white backdrop1, Blue Sky, and Stars. Click the cat in the sprite pane so you're writing code for the cat, not the stage.

💡 Tip

Can't find those exact backdrops? Any outdoor picture and any space picture will do. Just pick your own backdrop names in the dropdowns wherever you see ours.

#Step 2: Write the reset script

A movie has to start the same way every time you press play. These blocks put the cat back on its starting mark, at normal size, facing right, with no leftover effects:

Click the green flag. The blue sky appears, and the cat sits near the bottom-left corner. Now drag the cat somewhere silly and click the flag again. It jumps right back. That's what a reset script is for.

Each block undoes something the story changes later: the backdrop, the hiding, the shrinking, the ghost and color effects, the spin, the costume, and the position. When you add a new trick to a project, add the block that undoes it to the reset.

#Step 3: Walk into the park

Now the cat walks in, switching costumes so its legs move. Keep adding these to the bottom of the same script:

Click the flag. The cat takes four steps to the right, legs flipping each time.

Where does it stop? It started at x = -200 and moved 30 steps four times. That's -200 + 120 = -80. Look at the x box in the sprite pane to check. You'll need that number in Step 5.

Yes, that was the same three blocks four times. Lots of dragging! Next week the repeat block will do it for us in three blocks.

#Step 4: The cat talks

Add a speech bubble, a thought bubble, and a countdown:

Click the flag and watch everything so far. The cat walks in, says "What a nice day.", thinks about the stars, and counts down. Each bubble waits two seconds before the next block runs, so they never overlap.

#Step 5: Blast off

The cat zooms straight up and disappears out of the top:

The x stays at -80, the same spot the cat is standing on, so it flies straight up instead of drifting sideways. A short glide, only half a second, makes it feel fast. The one-second wait is a pause in the movie, like the screen going quiet before the next scene.

⚠️ Watch out

Scratch won't let a sprite glide all the way off the stage. It always keeps a little piece of it showing at the edge. That's why we hide the cat once it reaches the top.

#Step 6: Scene 2, in space

Switch to the starry backdrop. While the cat is still hidden, move it to the bottom and make it small and faint. Then show it and let it float up:

Why move and shrink the cat before show? It's what a stage crew does: set everything up while the curtain is closed. Right now these blocks run so quickly that you might not spot the difference, but the moment you add a pause between them (a wait for a dramatic scene change, say), anything that happens after show happens in front of the audience.

The ghost effect goes from 0 (solid) to 100 (invisible), so 30 makes the cat a little see-through, like something seen from a long way off.

#Step 7: The ending

Finish with a slow spin and a glow:

Four quarter turns make one full circle, so the cat ends up facing right again. The short waits let you see each quarter turn. Without them, all four turns would happen before the screen redraws, and the cat would seem to stand still. The color change makes the cat glow, as if space changed it.

#The whole script

Here's everything in order, top to bottom. Yours should match, except for any words you changed:

#Test it like a movie director

Click the green flag twice in a row. Does the movie look exactly the same both times? If the second showing starts in space, or with a tiny or invisible cat, a reset block is missing. These are the usual suspects:

  • The second run starts in space. switch backdrop to (Blue Sky v) is missing from the top.
  • The cat is invisible on the second run. show is missing from the reset, so it stayed hidden from the end of Scene 1.
  • The cat is tiny or faint on the second run. set size to (100) % or clear graphic effects is missing.
  • The cat flies off at an angle. The x in the blast-off glide doesn't match where the cat is standing. It should be -80.
  • The cat finishes upside down. You have three or five turn blocks instead of four.

Decisions in this build

3 questions

1You delete the hide block after the blast-off glide. What does the audience see during the one-second pause before space?

  • Without hide, nothing makes the cat invisible, and a glide can't carry it fully off the stage.

  • Scratch always keeps part of a sprite on the stage, so the cat's bottom half peeks down from the top until the scene changes.

  • Nothing in the script moves the cat down during the wait. It stays where the glide left it.

Show answer

B. Scratch always keeps part of a sprite on the stage, so the cat's bottom half peeks down from the top until the scene changes.

2Why does the blast-off glide go to x: -80 instead of x: 0?

  • If only y changes, the glide is a straight vertical line.

  • Any number works in a glide. 0 would just make the cat fly up and to the right at the same time.

  • The top is y = 180. -80 is an x value, a spot left of the middle.

Show answer

A. If only y changes, the glide is a straight vertical line.

3You take clear graphic effects out of the reset script and play the movie three times. What happens on the third run?

  • Clicking the flag doesn't reset anything by itself. Only reset blocks do.

  • The ghost and color effects stay after a run ends. Each run adds 50 more color on top of what was left.

  • Each run sets ghost to 30 instead of adding to it, so it stays at 30. It's the color that keeps changing.

Show answer

B. The ghost and color effects stay after a run ends. Each run adds 50 more color on top of what was left.

Key takeaways

  • Plan a story as scenes first, then build one scene at a time and test as you go.
  • A reset script puts back everything the story changes: backdrop, position, direction, costume, size, effects, and visibility.
  • Do your teleporting and shrinking while a sprite is hidden, then show it.
  • Scratch can't push a sprite fully off the stage, so hide it when it exits.
  • A wait between quick changes (costumes or turns) is what makes them visible.

#Make it yours

  • Change what the cat says, or swap the cat for a different sprite from the library.
  • Add a third scene: switch to a planet backdrop and have the cat land with a glide from the top.
  • Add a sound to the blast-off. The Sounds library has a whole Space category.

Save your project as week1-space-cat.sb3, or click File > Save now if you have an account.

  • Costume on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how costumes work and how to edit them.
  • Backdrop on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): adding, painting, and switching stage backgrounds.
  • Glide () Secs to X: () Y: () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): everything about the glide block.

What you'll learn

  • Send a sprite to exact spots with go to and glide.
  • Predict where a sprite will land by adding up change x and change y numbers.

Every exercise here uses something from this week's Notes. Build your answer first, click the green flag, and only then open the hint. Open the solution last, to compare. There's usually more than one right answer, so if yours does what the task asks, it's correct, even if it looks different from ours.

Start each exercise with a fresh project (File > New) unless it says otherwise.

#Warm-up: read the map

Drag the cat to each corner of the stage, one at a time, and read the x and y boxes in the sprite pane. Which corner has both numbers negative? Which has both positive? (Answer: bottom left is negative and negative, top right is positive and positive.) Now drag it until both boxes say 0. Where is it?

#Exercise 1: Center stage

Make the cat jump to the exact middle of the stage and say "Ta-da!" for 2 seconds when the green flag is clicked. Drag the cat into a corner before you test, to prove it really moves.

Need a hint?

The middle of the stage is the spot where x and y are both zero.

Show solution

Wherever you leave the cat, the flag sends it to (0, 0), and it says "Ta-da!" for 2 seconds.

#Exercise 2: Predict the landing spot

Don't build this one yet. Read it and work out, on paper or in your head, where the cat ends up:

Write down your answer as (x, y). Then build the script, click the flag, and check the x and y boxes in the sprite pane.

Need a hint?

Keep two running totals, one for x and one for y. change x only touches the x total, and change y only touches the y total. Start x at -100 and y at 50.

Show solution

The cat lands at (20, -50).

The order of the blocks doesn't change the final spot here, because each block only adds to one number. It would change the path the cat takes, though, if you added waits to watch it.

#Exercise 3: Corner tour

Make the cat visit all four corners, gliding one second to each, then come back to the middle. Use these spots so the cat stays fully on the stage:

Corner x y
top left -200 140
top right 200 140
bottom right 200 -140
bottom left -200 -140
Need a hint?

Start with a go to that puts the cat in the middle. Then you need five glide blocks: four corners and the trip home.

Show solution

The cat slides to each corner clockwise, then back to the middle, in 5 seconds. Going the other way around is fine too, as long as it hits all four.

#Exercise 4: Frog hops

Add the Frog sprite from the library (delete the cat, or keep it as an audience). The frog starts at x: -180, y: -100 and does three hops to the right. Each hop goes up 60, over 60, and back down 60. Make sure you can actually see each hop.

Need a hint?

change y by moves up and down, and change x by moves sideways. If the frog just slides to the right without hopping, Scratch is running the blocks too fast to see. What block slows things down?

Show solution

Each hop is up, pause, over, pause, down, pause. Three hops means the same six blocks three times.

The frog ends at x = 0, because -180 + 60 + 60 + 60 = 0. Without the waits, all three hops finish before the screen redraws, and the frog seems to teleport 180 steps to the right. Counting the hat, that's twenty blocks for three hops. Next week a loop will do the same job in nine.

#Exercise 5: The balloon that pops

Use the Balloon1 sprite. When the green flag is clicked:

  1. Reset it to size 50% with no effects, and make sure it's showing.
  2. Make it grow by 30 three times, with half a second between each.
  3. Make it say "Uh oh..." for 1 second.
  4. Play its Pop sound and make it disappear.

Click the flag a second time. The balloon must come back!

Need a hint?

Look at the very first thing your script does. If the balloon is hidden at the end of run one, what makes it appear on run two?

Show solution

The balloon grows from 50% to 80%, 110%, and 140%, worries out loud, then pops and vanishes. The show at the top is the key: without it the balloon stays hidden forever after the first run.

We used start sound so the balloon disappears at the same moment the pop begins. Want a slow fade instead of a pop? Replace hide with three change [ghost v] effect by (30) blocks, each followed by a short wait.

#Exercise 6: Good night

Add two backdrops: one daytime picture and one nighttime picture (for example Blue Sky and Stars). When the flag is clicked, the cat should:

  1. Start in the daytime backdrop, looking normal.
  2. Say "Time for bed!" for 2 seconds.
  3. Switch to the nighttime backdrop.
  4. Get darker, using the brightness effect.
  5. Think "Zzz..." for 3 seconds.
Need a hint?

Find set [color v] effect to (0) in Looks and open its dropdown. Brightness runs from -100 (black) to 100 (white). Which side means "darker"?

Show solution

Negative brightness darkens the cat, so it looks like the lights went out. clear graphic effects near the top brings back the daytime cat on the next run. Try -80 for a nearly black cat.

#Challenge: A two-sprite conversation

Add a second sprite (any character) and make the two of them talk, taking turns:

Each sprite needs its own green flag script, and both scripts start at the same moment. That's the tricky part: while one sprite talks, the other has to stay quiet for exactly as long. Plan it with this picture first:

Need a hint?

Use say [] for (2) seconds for every line, and the wait () seconds block from Control for the quiet parts. The friend's first line starts 2 seconds after the flag. How long must the cat wait between its two lines?

Show solution

Every line is 2 seconds, so every quiet part is a 2-second wait.

Click the friend sprite in the sprite pane, then build its script there:

This works, but try changing the cat's first line to 3 seconds. Now the friend interrupts! Lining up waits by hand breaks every time you change a line. In Week 4 you'll learn broadcasts, which let one sprite tell the other "your turn" instead.

Save your favorite answer as week1-practice.sb3.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Start scripts with event hat blocks: the green flag, a key, a click, or a backdrop change.
  • Give one sprite several scripts that run at the same time.
  • Repeat blocks a set number of times with repeat, or nonstop with forever.
  • Build an animation from next costume, wait, and a loop.
  • Choose between start sound and play sound until done.

Open any video game and leave the controller alone. Nothing happens. The hero just stands there, waiting. Press the right arrow and the hero runs; press space and it jumps. The game was listening the whole time, and each button press started a different piece of code.

Those button presses are called events, and this week your projects start listening for them. Here's a cat you can steer and tickle. Every stack starts with a different yellow hat block:

Click the flag, then press the arrow keys and click the cat. Each action runs just the script with the matching hat.

#Hat blocks wait for something to happen

Hat blocks live in the yellow Events category. A hat sits on top of a script and waits. When its event happens, the blocks under it run.

Hat block Runs when...
when green flag clicked someone clicks the green flag
when [space v] key pressed someone presses that key (pick any key in the dropdown)
when this sprite clicked someone clicks this sprite
when backdrop switches to [backdrop1 v] the stage changes to that backdrop
when stage clicked someone clicks an empty part of the stage (you'll only find this one on the Stage)

A sprite can have as many scripts as you like, each with its own hat, and they all wait at the same time. That's how one cat can walk with the arrow keys and talk when you click it.

Keep scripts spread out in the code area so you can read each one. If they start to overlap, right-click an empty spot and choose Clean up Blocks.

⚠️ Watch out

When the cat faces left with point in direction (-90), it turns upside down, because a sprite's normal rotation style is "all around." The set rotation style [left-right v] block from Motion, in the green flag script above, fixes it: now the cat flips to face left instead of rolling over.

#Holding a key down

Hold the right arrow and watch closely: the cat moves once, pauses, and then keeps going. That pause is your keyboard's key repeat, the same pause you get when you hold a letter down while typing. It's fine for now. Next week you'll learn a smoother way that games use.

#repeat: do it this many times

Last week the frog needed twenty blocks to hop three times, because each hop was the same six blocks over again. Loops fix that. They're the C-shaped blocks in Control. Any blocks you put inside the mouth of the C get repeated.

repeat (10) runs the blocks inside it exactly that many times, then moves on to whatever is under the loop.

The cat walks ten steps to the right, legs flipping each time. That's 10 × 20 = 200 steps, so it stops at x = 0. Only then does the say block run, because Scratch finishes the loop before moving on.

Want 20 steps instead of 10? Change one number. Stacking blocks by hand would mean dragging thirty more.

#forever: keep going until stop

forever repeats the blocks inside it over and over until you click the red stop sign. Look at its bottom edge: it's flat, with no bump. Nothing can snap under it, because nothing under a forever loop would ever get its turn.

The cat walks in place forever, as if it's on a treadmill.

#The animation recipe: costume + wait + loop

That little script is the heart of almost every Scratch animation:

  1. next costume changes the picture.
  2. wait slows it down enough for your eyes to see it. A smaller number means a faster animation.
  3. A loop keeps it going.

Many library sprites come with costumes drawn for exactly this. Add the Bat, the Parrot, or Butterfly 1 and open its Costumes tab to see the frames.

#Bounce around the stage

Put if on edge, bounce inside a forever loop and a sprite will zoom around the stage, turning back whenever it hits an edge:

Direction 45 is halfway between up and right, so the cat moves at an angle and bounces off all four edges like an old screensaver, until you click stop.

#Two ways to play a sound

Sound blocks are pink. Each sprite has its own sounds (the cat comes with Meow), and you can add more from the Sounds tab with the Choose a Sound button at the bottom left.

There are two blocks that play a sound, and the difference is all about timing:

  • start sound (Meow v) begins the sound and immediately moves on to the next block.
  • play sound (Meow v) until done waits until the sound has finished before moving on.

Try both of these on the cat, then press a and b:

Press a: you hear the meow and see the bubble at the same moment. Press b: you hear the meow first, and the bubble shows up only after it ends.

Use start sound when a sound should go with an action, like a boing as a sprite jumps. Use play sound until done when things must happen in order, like the notes of a song.

#Make a staircase of meows

Put a sound in a loop and change its pitch each time around. Each 10 of pitch is about one key higher on a piano:

Press space and the cat climbs a staircase: five meows, each one higher. The set block at the top and clear sound effects at the bottom keep the next press from starting high.

Other handy sound blocks: stop all sounds, set volume to (100) %, and change volume by (-10).

#What usually goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

A loop runs too fast to see. Ten costume changes with no wait inside the loop flicker past in a blink. Add a wait inside the loop, not after it.

  • A block won't snap under forever. That's on purpose. Put it above the loop, or in a separate script.
  • The wrong blocks are repeating. Only blocks inside the C repeat. Drag blocks in or out until the loop holds exactly what you want.
  • The music sounds squashed. You used start sound inside a loop. The loop doesn't wait, so each pass cuts the sound off and restarts it. Use play sound until done.
  • Pressing a key does nothing. Click on the stage once, so the keyboard goes to Scratch and not to some other part of the page.

#Check yourself

The cat starts in the middle, facing right.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does Script A do?

  • The say block is under the loop, not inside it, so it runs only once.

  • The loop runs four times (4 × 25 = 100), and only then does Scratch reach the say block.

  • Blocks run top to bottom, and a loop finishes before the next block starts.

Show answer

B. The loop runs four times (4 × 25 = 100), and only then does Scratch reach the say block.

2You press space with Script B. When does the bubble appear?

  • That's what start sound would do. "Until done" makes the script wait.

  • play sound until done holds the script until the sound ends, then the say block runs.

  • The bubble does appear. It just waits its turn.

Show answer

B. play sound until done holds the script until the sound ends, then the say block runs.

3You click the green flag with Script C. What happens?

  • Each script runs on its own. One forever loop doesn't block a different script.

  • Both scripts start when the flag is clicked, and Scratch runs them side by side.

  • The color loop is a forever loop too, so it keeps changing the color the whole time.

Show answer

B. Both scripts start when the flag is clicked, and Scratch runs them side by side.

4You drag say [Bye!] for (2) seconds under a forever loop. What happens?

  • Nothing after a forever loop would ever run, so Scratch doesn't let you put anything there.

  • The stop sign stops every script, including that one.

  • Blocks run top to bottom, so something under the loop could never come first.

Show answer

A. Nothing after a forever loop would ever run, so Scratch doesn't let you put anything there.

Key takeaways

  • Hat blocks in Events wait for something to happen (the flag, a key, a click, a backdrop change), then run their script.
  • One sprite can have many scripts, and scripts with the same hat run at the same time.
  • repeat (n) runs its inside n times and then moves on. forever never moves on, so nothing goes under it.
  • Animation is next costume + wait + a loop.
  • start sound doesn't wait. play sound until done waits for the sound to finish.

#Further reading

  • Events Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every yellow hat block, with examples.
  • Forever on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how the forever loop works, and why nothing fits under it.
  • Sound Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): all the pink blocks, including pitch and pan effects.

What you'll learn

  • Put scripts on the Stage as well as on a sprite.
  • Loop background music without it cutting off.
  • Run several forever loops at once without them getting in each other's way.
  • Build "do it, then undo it" moves (a jump and a pulse) from two matching repeat loops.

Turn the music up. Today you're building a dance party where the music never stops, the lights flash, and you're the DJ. Arrow keys slide the dancer around, space makes it jump, up arrow makes it pulse to the beat, and clicking it makes it sing. Almost every piece uses this week's three ideas, events, loops, and sounds, all at once.

Here's who does what. Seven scripts, two of them on the Stage:

Who Starts with What it does
Stage green flag plays music forever
Stage green flag switches backdrops every 2 seconds
Cat green flag resets, then dances in place forever
Cat left and right arrows slides left and right
Cat space jumps
Cat up arrow grows and shrinks in a quick pulse
Cat a click changes color and meows

And here's how they play together after you click the flag. The three loops run side by side, and the key and click scripts jump in whenever you press something:

#Step 1: Set up the dance floor

Start a new project (File > New).

  1. Click Choose a Backdrop and add three party backdrops. Party, Concert, Spotlight, and Neon Tunnel all work well.
  2. Click the Stage button (bottom right), then open the Backdrops tab.
  3. Right-click the plain white backdrop1 and choose delete, so a blank white screen doesn't flash up during the light show.

#Step 2: Loop the music

With the Stage still selected, open the Sounds tab. Click Choose a Sound, click the Loops category at the top, and choose a song. We used Dance Celebrate, but any loop works.

Go to the Code tab (still on the Stage) and build this:

Click the green flag. The music plays, and when the song ends it starts right over. Click the stop sign to stop it.

⚠️ Watch out

Use play sound until done here, not start sound. A forever loop with start sound never waits, so it restarts the song again and again, many times a second. All you'd hear is a buzz or a stutter of the first moment of the song.

Why put the music on the Stage instead of the cat? The music belongs to the whole party, not one dancer. If you delete the cat or add five more dancers later, the music keeps going.

#Step 3: Flash the lights

Still on the Stage, add a second script. Both Stage scripts start when you click the flag, and they run at the same time:

Click the flag. The music plays, and every 2 seconds the backdrop changes. After the last backdrop, next backdrop goes back around to the first one, so the light show never runs out.

#Step 4: The dancer

Click the cat in the sprite pane. This first script resets the cat, then makes it dance in place forever:

Click the flag. The cat stands in the middle and steps in place, switching costumes about three times a second.

💡 Tip

Make the dance match the music. Tap your foot to the song and change the wait number until the cat's steps land on the beat. Try 0.25 or 0.5.

#Step 5: Slide with the arrow keys

Add two new scripts to the cat, each with its own key hat:

Press the arrows. The cat slides left and right and faces the way it's going. Because Step 4 set the rotation style to left-right, it flips to face left instead of turning upside down. And notice the dance keeps going while it slides: that's two scripts running at once on the same sprite.

#Step 6: Jump!

A jump is two loops: one going up and one coming down.

Press space. The cat rises 100 steps (10 times 10) and comes back down to exactly where it started. Both loops use the same numbers, so the landing spot always matches the takeoff spot.

Try pressing space again while the cat is in the air. Nothing happens! Scratch won't restart a key script that's still running, so the cat finishes its first jump before it can start another.

#Step 7: The pulse move

Make the cat swell and shrink when you press the up arrow:

The cat grows from 100% to 150% and back again in a quick pulse. It's the same pattern as the jump: do something, then undo it the same number of times.

#Step 8: Click to sing

Last script. When you click the cat, it should meow while the dance keeps going:

Click the cat. It shifts to a new color, meows, and says "Meow!" for a second, and the music and dancing never stop. We chose start sound here because the meow and the bubble should happen at the same moment.

#Test the whole party

Click the green flag and try everything:

  • Music plays without stopping, and the backdrop changes every 2 seconds.
  • The cat dances in place.
  • Left and right slide it, space makes it jump, and up arrow makes it pulse.
  • Clicking it changes its color and makes it meow.
  • The stop sign stops everything.

Now click the green flag again. The cat should go back to the middle with its normal color and size. If it doesn't, check the reset blocks at the top of Step 4.

#Common bugs

  • No music, or the song isn't in the dropdown. You added the sound to the cat instead of the Stage. Each sprite and the Stage have their own sounds. Add the song to the Stage too, or move the music script onto the cat.
  • The cat lands lower after each jump. The two jump loops don't match. Both should repeat 10 times by 10.
  • The cat gets bigger every time it pulses. The two pulse loops don't match. Check the counts and the numbers.
  • Pressing space scrolls the web page. Click on the stage once so Scratch gets the key presses.

Decisions in this build

3 questions

1Why does the music loop use play sound until done instead of start sound?

  • "Until done" holds the loop on each pass, so the song plays all the way through, then repeats.

  • Both blocks work on the Stage. The difference is whether the loop waits.

  • Neither block changes the volume. That's set volume to (100) %.

Show answer

A. "Until done" holds the loop on each pass, so the song plays all the way through, then repeats.

2Your jump goes up with repeat (10) and change y by (10), but comes down with repeat (8) and change y by (-10). What happens after three jumps?

  • It only lands at the start if the up and down trips are the same size.

  • Each jump goes up 100 and down only 80, so it ends 20 higher. Three jumps leaves it 60 steps up.

  • It comes down less than it went up, so it drifts upward, not downward.

Show answer

B. Each jump goes up 100 and down only 80, so it ends 20 higher. Three jumps leaves it 60 steps up.

3You click the cat while it's dancing. Why doesn't the dance stop?

  • They're separate scripts, each with its own hat block.

  • Scratch runs each script on its own, so starting one doesn't stop another.

  • start sound never pauses anything. That's why we picked it.

Show answer

B. Scratch runs each script on its own, so starting one doesn't stop another.

Key takeaways

  • The Stage can have scripts and sounds too. Put things that belong to the whole scene, like music, there.
  • Several forever loops can run at once, even on the same sprite.
  • Loop background music with play sound until done, so each pass waits for the song to end.
  • "Do it, then undo it" moves like jumps and pulses need two loops that match exactly.
  • A key script that's still running won't restart, so a jump always finishes before the next one.

#Make it yours

  • Add a second dancer from the library, with its own dance loop and its own keys, like w, a, and d.
  • Use when backdrop switches to [Spotlight v] on the cat to do a special move whenever the spotlight comes on.
  • Add a key that runs stop all sounds for a dramatic pause. What happens to the music loop after it?
