What you'll learn

  • Start scripts with keys, clicks, stage clicks, and backdrop changes.
  • Replace stacks of repeated blocks with a repeat loop.
  • Combine moving, costume changes, and bouncing inside one forever loop.
  • Keep a steady beat with sounds and waits.
  • Put one loop inside another.
  • Run two loops with different timing on the same sprite.

Every challenge here uses at least one event hat block, and most use a loop. Build it, test it with the green flag (or the key or click it listens for), then compare with the solution. If your version works but looks different, that's normal: programmers solve the same problem in lots of ways.

#Warm-up: squash the frog

Remember last week's frog, with twenty blocks for three hops? Rebuild it with a repeat (3) loop. Put the six blocks of one hop inside the loop, and keep the go to above it. You should end up with nine blocks, counting the hat. Then change 3 to 6 and watch the frog cross the whole stage. (Start it at x: -220 so it has room.)

#Exercise 1: Four-way arrows

The dance party only slid left and right. Make the cat move in all four directions with the arrow keys, 10 steps at a time. Add a green flag script that puts the cat in the middle.

Need a hint?

You need five scripts: one green flag script and one for each arrow key. change x by moves sideways and change y by moves up and down, without the cat having to turn.

Show solution

Each arrow nudges the cat 10 steps that way, and holding a key keeps it going after the usual key-repeat pause. Because we used change x by and change y by instead of move, the cat never turns. It faces right even while it walks up.

#Exercise 2: Click to spin

When you click the cat, it should spin around one full circle, smoothly, and then say "Wheee!" for 1 second.

Need a hint?

One full circle is 360 degrees. If each turn is 15 degrees, how many turns do you need? Put one turn block inside a repeat loop so you can watch each small turn.

Show solution

360 ÷ 15 = 24, so the loop repeats 24 times.

The cat spins once all the way around, ends facing right, and says "Wheee!"

Why point in direction (90) at the top? Click the cat twice quickly. A new click restarts a sprite-clicked script that's already running, so without that block the second spin would start from wherever the first one got to, and the cat would finish tilted. Pointing right first makes every spin start from the same place.

If the cat doesn't spin at all, an earlier script may have set its rotation style to left-right. Add set rotation style [all around v] at the top.

#Exercise 3: Flapping bat

Add the Bat sprite from the library and delete the cat. When the green flag is clicked, the bat flies back and forth across the stage forever, flapping its wings the whole time. It must never fly upside down.

Need a hint?

One forever loop can do several jobs on each pass: move a little, show the next costume, and check the edge. Which Motion block stops a sprite from turning upside down?

Show solution

The bat flies right, flapping, turns around at the edge, flies left, and keeps going until you click stop. Its four costumes are drawn as wing positions, so next costume is all the flapping takes. Try wait (0.1) seconds for a lazier bat.

#Exercise 4: A metronome

A metronome ticks at a steady beat to help musicians keep time. Make one:

  1. Add the Pop sound to a sprite (Sounds tab, Choose a Sound).
  2. When the green flag is clicked, play Pop once every half second, forever.
  3. Make the sprite change color a little on every tick, so you can see the beat too.
Need a hint?

The wait block should decide the timing, not the sound. Which sound block starts a sound without making the script wait for it?

Show solution

Pop, pop, pop: two ticks every second, while the sprite slowly cycles through colors. start sound doesn't wait, so the half-second wait sets the beat exactly. Try wait (0.25) seconds for a beat twice as fast.

#Exercise 5: Day and night switch

Add two backdrops, one day and one night (like Blue Sky and Stars). Make these two things happen:

  1. On the Stage: clicking the stage switches to the next backdrop.
  2. On the cat: when the backdrop switches to night, the cat says "Good night!" for 2 seconds. When it switches to day, it says "Good morning!" for 2 seconds.
Need a hint?

Click the Stage button and look in its Events blocks for a hat that only the Stage has. On the cat, there's a hat that runs when the backdrop changes, no matter who changed it.

Show solution

Click an empty part of the stage and the scene changes. The cat greets the new time of day. Notice the cat never checks who switched the backdrop. It just reacts to the change. Pick your own backdrop names in the dropdowns if they're different.

#Exercise 6: Walk a square

Make the cat walk around a square, 200 steps on each side, and end up exactly where it started. The legs don't need to move. Here's the catch: use two loops, one inside the other.

Need a hint?

Walking one side is "move a little, many times." Then the cat turns 90 degrees. A square is four sides, so "walk a side, then turn" happens four times. Which loop goes on the outside?

Show solution

The inside loop walks one side (10 × 20 = 200 steps). The outside loop does that four times, turning after each side. The cat goes right, up, left, and down, and ends at (-100, -100) facing right, where it began.

On the way around, the cat tips onto its side and then upside down, because its rotation style is "all around." Add set rotation style [don't rotate v] at the top if you'd rather it stayed upright.

#Challenge: Fish tank

Build a fish tank:

  • Use an underwater backdrop, like Underwater 1, and the Fish sprite.
  • The fish swims around forever, bouncing off the edges, without going upside down.
  • It shouldn't follow the same zigzag every time. Make it wander. (Look in Operators for pick random (1) to (10).)
  • At the same time, the fish makes a bubble sound every 3 seconds. The Fish sprite already has a sound called bubbles.

The tricky part is timing. The swimming needs to update many times a second, but the sound only every 3 seconds. Put a wait (3) seconds in the swimming loop and the fish would freeze for 3 seconds at a time. So give each job its own script:

Need a hint?

For wandering, put turn right (pick random (-10) to (10)) degrees inside the swimming loop. A random number between -10 and 10 means each step turns a tiny bit left or right, so the path is never the same twice.

Show solution

Two green flag scripts on the same sprite. One handles swimming, the other handles sound, and neither has to wait for the other.

The fish drifts across the tank in a wobbly path, bounces back from the walls, and never swims the same route twice. Every 3 seconds or so you hear bubbles, while the swimming carries on.

We left out next costume on purpose. The Fish sprite's four costumes are four different fish, not swimming frames, so switching them would turn your fish into a new fish every step. Open its Costumes tab to see.

Save your favorite as week2-practice.sb3.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Recognize boolean blocks (the pointy ones) and test whether they're true or false.
  • Use if <> then to run blocks only sometimes, and if <> then with else to choose between two paths.
  • Explain why game checks go inside a forever loop.
  • Move a sprite smoothly with key pressed?.
  • Ask the player a question and react to the answer.
  • Detect collisions with another sprite, a color, or the edge of the stage.

Every morning you make little decisions. If it's raining, take an umbrella; else, grab your sunglasses. Games make decisions like that all the time, many times every second. If the player touches the coin, collect it. If the ball reaches the wall, bounce. If the hero touches lava, start over.

Here's a cat that makes a decision about your mouse. Hover over it and it blushes and says hi. Move away and it goes back to normal:

By the end of this page you'll know what every piece of that does, and how to use the same pattern for walls, coins, and finish lines.

#Yes-or-no questions

Some blocks have pointed ends, like a stretched hexagon. They're called boolean blocks, or conditions. They don't do anything by themselves. They answer a yes-or-no question with true or false.

From Sensing:

  • <touching (mouse-pointer v)?> asks: is this sprite touching the mouse pointer? (The dropdown also lists edge and every other sprite.)
  • <touching color [#ff0000]?> asks: is this sprite touching that color?
  • <key (space v) pressed?> asks: is that key being held down right now?
  • <mouse down?> asks: is the mouse button pressed?

From Operators, comparing numbers or words:

  • <(x position) > (200)> asks: is x bigger than 200?
  • <(x position) < (-200)> asks: is x smaller than -200?
  • <(answer) = [yes]> asks: is the answer exactly "yes"?

Click any boolean block in the palette and Scratch shows a little bubble saying true or false right now. Try it with touching (mouse-pointer v)?: set its dropdown to edge and click it while the cat is in the middle of the stage. Then drag the cat against a side of the stage and click it again.

#if then: run blocks only sometimes

The if <> then block in Control has a pointed hole in it, the same shape as a boolean block. Drop a condition into the hole. The blocks inside the if run only when the condition is true. When it's false, Scratch skips them.

An if checks once, at the moment Scratch reaches it. That's why the shy cat's if sits inside a forever loop: the loop sends Scratch back to ask the question again and again, many times a second.

This "forever-if" pattern is how almost every game watches for things to happen. You'll use it in every project from here on.

#if else: pick one of two paths

The bigger if <> then block has a second mouth labeled else. Every time Scratch reaches it, exactly one of the two parts runs: the top part if the condition is true, the bottom part if it's false. Never both, never neither.

Look at the shy cat again. With only an if, the cat would say "Hi there!" when you hovered, but the bubble would stay forever after you moved away, because nothing tells it to stop. The else part handles "not touching": say [] with an empty bubble clears the speech, and clear graphic effects puts the color back.

#Smooth movement with key pressed?

Last week you moved the cat with when [right arrow v] key pressed. It works, but you noticed the pause before the key starts repeating. Games use a forever loop with key pressed? instead:

Now the cat glides smoothly the instant you press a key, with no pause. And since all four ifs are checked on every pass, holding up and right together moves it diagonally.

#Ask a question, use the answer

ask [What's your name?] and wait shows a question with a text box at the bottom of the stage, and the script waits until the player types something and presses Enter. Whatever they typed is stored in the answer block (in Sensing), which you can use like any other value:

Type yes and the cat says "Me too!" Type no, or anything else at all, and it says "More for me, then!" The = block ignores capital letters, so YES and Yes count as yes. Spelling still matters, though: yeah is not yes.

#Collisions: when things touch

A collision is when two things on the stage overlap. Scratch gives you three main ways to notice one.

#Touching another sprite

Pick the other sprite's name in the touching dropdown. Here the cat chases your mouse, and when you lead it to a sprite called Apple, it eats:

After each bite, the cat jumps to a random spot, so you have to lead it back.

#Touching a color

touching color is perfect for walls, lava, and finish lines painted onto the backdrop. To set the color, click the color circle in the block, click the eyedropper at the bottom of the color menu, and then click that color on the stage. The eyedropper picks the exact color, which matters: a red that's slightly different won't count.

If the sprite touches red, it goes back to the start. Like every check, it needs to live inside a forever loop to keep watching.

#Touching the edge, or an invisible wall

<touching (edge v)?> turns true when any part of the sprite reaches the side of the stage. For a wall that isn't at the edge, check the sprite's position yourself:

The cat walks right but stops dead at x = 200, as if it bumped into glass. Every time it steps past, the second if puts it back on the line before the screen even redraws.

💡 Tip

if on edge, bounce is a handy shortcut, but it only works for the four edges of the stage. To bounce off a paddle or a wall sprite, check if <touching (Paddle v)?> then and turn the sprite yourself.

#What usually goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

The if only works once. You forgot the forever loop around it, so Scratch asked the question one time, at the start, and never again. Wrap the if in a forever.

  • touching color never turns true. The colors don't match exactly. Use the eyedropper instead of picking a color by eye.
  • The sprite gets stuck in a wall. After a collision, move it back out (for example, change x by (-5)), so it isn't still touching the wall on the next check.
  • It seems like both parts of an if/else ran. You probably used two separate if blocks instead of one if else. Two ifs can both run. The two halves of an if else never can.
  • The sprite's own name isn't in the touching dropdown. A sprite can't check whether it's touching itself, so its own name never appears. If you see the wrong list, you're editing the wrong sprite.

#Check yourself

Check your understanding

4 questions

1With Script A, the mouse is far from the cat when you click the flag. A few seconds later you move the mouse onto the cat. What happens?

  • It would, if the if were inside a forever loop. Here it was checked only once.

  • The if asked its question at the moment the flag was clicked. The answer was false, the script ended, and nobody asks again.

  • There's no loop, so nothing repeats.

Show answer

B. The if asked its question at the moment the flag was clicked. The answer was false, the script ended, and nobody asks again.

2With Script B, you hold space for one second and then let go. What do you see?

  • While space is held, the top part runs on every pass and adds 5 each time. Once you let go, the else part runs instead and sets the size to 100.

  • The if is inside a forever, so it adds 5 on every pass while the key is held.

  • The else part runs as soon as space isn't pressed, and it resets the size.

Show answer

A. While space is held, the top part runs on every pass and adds 5 each time. Once you let go, the else part runs instead and sets the size to 100.

3With Script C, the player types four. What does the cat say?

  • Scratch doesn't turn words into numbers. To the = block, four and 4 are different.

  • The answer four isn't equal to 4, so the condition is false and the else part runs.

  • Any answer works. It just goes to the else part.

Show answer

B. The answer four isn't equal to 4, so the condition is false and the else part runs.

4Your maze walls are blue rectangles painted on the backdrop. Which condition tells the player it hit a wall?

  • edge means only the four sides of the stage, not walls drawn inside it.

  • The walls are part of the backdrop, not a sprite, so you detect them by their color.

  • There's no sprite called Wall. The walls are painted on the backdrop, so they won't show up in this dropdown.

Show answer

B. The walls are part of the backdrop, not a sprite, so you detect them by their color.

Key takeaways

  • Boolean blocks have pointed ends and answer yes-or-no questions with true or false.
  • if <> then runs its blocks only when the condition is true. With else, exactly one of the two parts runs.
  • An if checks once. Put it inside forever to keep checking: that's the forever-if pattern.
  • key pressed? in a forever loop gives smooth movement with no key-repeat pause.
  • ask and wait stores what the player types in answer, and = ignores capital letters.
  • Detect collisions with touching (sprite)?, touching color? (use the eyedropper), touching (edge)?, or by checking x position and y position.

#Further reading

  • Sensing Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every light blue block, including touching, ask, and key pressed.
  • If () Then, Else on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how if/else chooses between two paths, with examples.
  • Touching ()? on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): collisions with sprites, the edge, and the mouse pointer.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Paint a maze backdrop with walls in one color.
  • Move a player smoothly with key pressed? inside a forever loop.
  • Make walls solid with the "move, check, undo" trick.
  • Send the player back to the start when it touches the edge.
  • Use distance to with if else so the goal reacts as the player gets close.

Mazes are one of the oldest computer games, and they make a great first real game. Today you'll paint your own maze, then write the code that makes it play like one: walls you can't walk through, edges that send you back to the start, and a spinning star at the end that shouts "Almost there!" as you get close. When you're done, you can hand the keyboard to someone else and watch them try.

Here's the whole game as a picture. Each arrow is something that can happen while you play:

#Step 1: Paint the maze

The walls are part of the backdrop, so you paint them on the Stage.

  1. Start a new project (File > New).
  2. Click the Stage button in the bottom right, then open the Backdrops tab.
  3. Choose the Rectangle tool. Set Fill to one bright color, like blue, and set Outline to the same blue (or to no outline). Use this one color for every wall.
  4. Draw thick wall rectangles that make a path from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. Keep the path wide, at least two fingers wide on your screen.

💡 Tip

Make your first maze easy, with three or four turns. A maze that's too hard to test is a maze you can't finish building. You can paint a harder one once the code works.

Why one color for every wall? The code will check for a single exact color. A wall in a slightly different blue, or with a black outline, won't count as a wall.

#Step 2: Add the player and the goal

  1. Delete the cat: right-click it in the sprite pane and choose delete.
  2. Add the Ball sprite from the library. In the sprite pane, rename it Player and set its Size to 40.
  3. Drag the player to the start of your maze, at the top left. Write down the x and y in the sprite pane. We'll use x: -200, y: 140.
  4. Add the Star sprite (or any sprite you like) and rename it Goal. Drag it to the end of the maze at the bottom right. We'll use x: 200, y: -140.

Renaming matters. The touching and distance to dropdowns list sprites by name, and "Player" and "Goal" are much easier to read than "Ball" and "Star".

#Step 3: Move the player

Click the Player sprite. Build a reset and the smooth movement loop from the Notes, with steps of 3 so the ball is easy to steer through narrow spots:

Click the green flag and steer with the arrows. The player moves smoothly... and drives straight through your walls like a ghost. Time to fix that.

#Step 4: Make the walls solid

Scratch has no "solid" setting for colors, so we fake it with a trick: move, check, undo. Take a step. If that step put the player inside a wall, take the same step backward, right away. It all happens before the screen redraws, so the player never looks like it entered the wall. It just looks like it stopped.

Put a touching color check inside each arrow's if. To set the color, click the color circle in the block, click the eyedropper at the bottom of the menu, then click one of your walls on the stage:

Do the same for the other three arrows. The undo is always the same number with the opposite sign:

Arrow Move Undo
right change x by (3) change x by (-3)
left change x by (-3) change x by (3)
up change y by (3) change y by (-3)
down change y by (-3) change y by (3)

Test it. The player should stop at walls as if they're solid, and still slide along them when you hold two arrows at once.

Why check inside each arrow's if, instead of once at the bottom of the loop? Because each check has to know which step to undo. A single check at the bottom would know the player hit a wall, but not whether to back out left, right, up, or down.

⚠️ Watch out

If the player is stuck the moment the game starts, its starting spot overlaps a wall, so every move gets undone. Drag it to an open spot and update the numbers in go to x: () y: ().

#Step 5: The edge sends you back

If your maze has gaps at the side of the stage, a sneaky player could walk around the outside. Add this inside the forever loop, below the four arrow checks:

Now reaching the edge of the stage sends the player back to the start.

#Step 6: Win the game

Still inside the forever loop, add the goal check:

stop [all v] ends every script in the project, just like clicking the red stop sign.

#Step 7: The goal cheers you on

Click the Goal sprite. This script spins the star slowly, and uses if else with distance to to cheer when the player is near:

distance to (Player v) is in Sensing. It reports how many steps away the player is, measured center to center. The star spins all the time, says "Almost there!" when the player is within 80 steps, and clears its bubble when the player wanders off.

#The complete Player script

Here's everything on the Player sprite. Your color may look different if you painted your walls another color.

#Playtest it

Play your maze start to finish three times, then check:

  • Can you get through any wall? (You shouldn't!)
  • Is there anywhere you get stuck with no way out? Widen that part of the path.
  • Does the star say "Almost there!" only when you're close?
  • Does reaching the star end the game?

Then hand it to someone else and watch them play without helping. Wherever they get confused or stuck is the next thing to fix.

#Common bugs

  • The player walks through walls. The color in touching color doesn't match your walls. Use the eyedropper again, and check that every wall is the same color.
  • The player can't move at all. It starts on top of a wall. Move the start spot.
  • Nothing happens at the star. The Goal check is outside the forever loop, or the touching dropdown shows a name other than Goal.
  • The star never cheers. The ball isn't named Player, or the distance to dropdown isn't set to Player.

Decisions in this build

3 questions

1When the player hits a wall moving right, why do we undo with change x by (-3) and not go to x: (-200) y: (140)?

  • The undo puts the player exactly where it was a moment ago, touching the wall but not inside it.

  • go to works anywhere. It just does the wrong job here: it's a penalty, not a wall.

  • The number undoes the step the player just took. It's 3 because each step is 3.

Show answer

A. The undo puts the player exactly where it was a moment ago, touching the wall but not inside it.

2You paint one wall dark blue and the rest light blue. What happens at the dark blue wall?

  • touching color checks one exact color. Dark blue and light blue are different colors to Scratch.

  • The check only matches the color you picked with the eyedropper, so the dark blue wall doesn't count.

  • Getting stuck happens when the player starts inside a wall it can detect. This wall isn't detected at all.

Show answer

B. The check only matches the color you picked with the eyedropper, so the dark blue wall doesn't count.

3You drag the Goal check out of the loop and drop it just above forever, right under the say block. What happens when you reach the star?

  • The check is no longer repeated, so it can't notice you arriving later.

  • At the start the player is far from the star, so the answer was false. Only checks inside forever keep asking.

  • At the start the player isn't touching the star, so the stop [all v] inside the check doesn't run.

Show answer

B. At the start the player is far from the star, so the answer was false. Only checks inside forever keep asking.

Key takeaways

  • Walls painted on the backdrop are detected by their color, so paint every wall in one exact color and set the check with the eyedropper.
  • "Move, check, undo" makes a wall feel solid: step, and if you're in the wall, step straight back.
  • Put each undo inside the matching arrow's if, so it knows which step to reverse.
  • Checks for walls, edges, and goals all belong inside the forever loop.
  • distance to plus if else lets a sprite react to how close another sprite is.

#Make it yours

  • Paint a red "lava" patch on the backdrop. Touching it sends the player back to start.
  • Add sounds: a start sound when the player bumps a wall, and a cheer at the star.
  • Paint a second, harder maze backdrop for later. In Week 6 you'll learn to switch levels.

Save your project as week3-maze.sb3, or click File > Save now. Next week, you'll add a timer and a score with variables.

#Further reading

  • Key () Pressed? on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how the key pressed condition works, and why it's smoother than the hat block.
  • Paint Editor on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every drawing tool, for building better mazes.
  • Touching Color ()? on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how color collisions work, and why exact colors matter.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use if else so a sprite is always in one of two states.
  • Check a typed answer with ask and wait and =.
  • Build invisible walls with x position and comparisons.
  • Detect a painted color and another sprite.
  • Find and fix a check that's in the wrong place.
  • Bounce a ball off a paddle and end the game when it's missed.

These challenges are where your projects start to feel like real games. Most of them use the forever-if pattern from the Notes: a forever loop with an if inside, asking its question over and over. Try each one before you open the hint. When you get stuck, ask yourself: "What question does my sprite need to keep asking?"

#Warm-up: true or false?

Find key (space v) pressed? in Sensing and click it. Scratch shows false. Now hold the space bar down while you click it. What does the bubble say? Then try touching (edge v)? twice: once with the cat in the middle, once after you drag it against a side of the stage.

#Exercise 1: Glow button

When the green flag is clicked, the cat should glow (color effect set to 50) only while the space bar is held down. The moment you let go, it goes back to normal.

Need a hint?

The cat is always in one of two states, glowing or normal. Which block picks exactly one of two choices, every time? It needs to keep checking, too.

Show solution

Hold space and the cat changes color. Let go and it's back to orange right away. A when [space v] key pressed hat couldn't do this job, because it can only notice a key going down, never a key coming back up.

#Exercise 2: Math quiz

When the green flag is clicked, the cat asks "What is 6 + 7?" If the player types 13, the cat plays its Meow sound and says "Correct!" Otherwise it says "Not quite. It's 13." Both messages last 2 seconds.

Need a hint?

ask [] and wait stores whatever was typed in the answer block. Put answer into one side of an = block from Operators.

Show solution

Type 13 and you get a meow and "Correct!" Type 12, or thirteen, and the cat corrects you. The start sound lets the meow and the bubble happen together.

#Exercise 3: The invisible fence

Make the cat move left and right smoothly with the arrow keys, 5 steps at a time, but never let it go past x = 150 on the right or x = -150 on the left. No drawing allowed: use x position and the > and < blocks from Operators.

Need a hint?

Let the cat take its step first. Then ask: "Am I past the fence?" If it is, which Motion block puts it right back on the line without changing its y?

Show solution

The cat slides while you hold the arrows and stops dead at x = 150 and x = -150. It never looks like it crossed the line, because the fix happens before the screen redraws.

#Exercise 4: The floor is lava

Paint a backdrop with a red strip along the bottom of the stage (Rectangle tool, red fill). Then:

  1. The cat starts at x: 0, y: 100.
  2. The arrow keys move it in all four directions, 4 steps at a time.
  3. If it touches the red lava, it says "Too hot!" for 1 second and goes back to the start.
Need a hint?

Start from the smooth four-way movement in the Notes. Add one more if inside the same forever loop, and set its color with the eyedropper by clicking your red strip.

Show solution

Steer into the red strip and the cat yelps "Too hot!", freezes for a second (the say ... for (1) seconds block makes the whole loop wait), and jumps back to its starting spot.

#Exercise 5: Snack time

Add the Apple sprite. The cat follows your mouse pointer. Whenever the cat touches the apple, the apple (not the cat!) plays its Chomp sound, says "Chomp!" for half a second, and jumps to a random spot.

Need a hint?

This needs one script on each sprite. The cat only chases. The apple keeps asking, "Is the cat touching me?" What's the cat's name in the apple's touching dropdown?

Show solution

The cat chases your mouse. When it reaches the apple, the apple crunches, says "Chomp!", and pops up somewhere new. Splitting the jobs like this keeps each script short: each sprite looks after itself.

The cat is still called Sprite1 unless you renamed it. If you did, pick its new name in the dropdown. And if the cat wobbles once it reaches the mouse, that's normal: it keeps stepping past the pointer and turning back.

#Exercise 6: Bug hunt

This script should make the cat say "Ouch!" and go back to the middle whenever it touches the edge. It moves fine, but it never says "Ouch!" Find the bug and fix it.

Need a hint?

Read it top to bottom, the way Scratch does. When does Scratch reach the edge check? Is the cat anywhere near the edge at that moment? Does Scratch ever come back to it?

Show solution

The edge check is outside the forever loop. It runs once, right after the cat goes to the middle, when it's nowhere near an edge. Then Scratch enters the loop and never comes back. Drag the whole if block into the loop:

Now the question gets asked on every pass, so the cat says "Ouch!" the moment it reaches either side. This is the single most common bug in Scratch games, so it's worth remembering what it looks like.

#Challenge: Paddle ball

Build a mini paddle game:

  • Paddle: add the Paddle sprite from the library. It sits near the bottom at y = -140 and follows the mouse left and right.
  • Ball: add the Ball sprite at 50% size. It starts near the middle, moves at an angle, and bounces off the top and sides.
  • When the ball hits the paddle, it bounces back up.
  • If the ball gets past the paddle (below y = -150), it says "Game over!" and the game stops.

Here are the states the ball can be in:

Need a hint?

The paddle only needs set x to (mouse x) in a forever loop. For the ball, to bounce up off a flat paddle use point in direction ((180) - (direction)): it flips a ball heading down into a ball heading up. Then think hard about the order of the checks inside the ball's loop. What should Scratch notice first, a missed ball or the bottom edge?

Show solution

The ball starts in the middle and heads down at an angle. It bounces off the walls, the top, and your paddle. Miss it, and the ball says "Game over!" and everything stops.

Why is the game over check above if on edge, bounce? The loop runs top to bottom. If the bounce came first, the ball could bounce off the bottom edge before the game ever noticed it got past you, and you could never lose.

Why the extra move (10) steps after hitting the paddle? It pushes the ball clear of the paddle. Without it, the ball might still be touching the paddle on the next pass, flip again, and head back down into it.

Next week, you'll add a score that goes up with every hit.

Save your favorite as week3-practice.sb3.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Make a variable, show it on the stage, and reset it when the green flag is clicked.
  • Count a score up, count lives down, and build a 30-second countdown clock.
  • Send a broadcast from one sprite and react to it in other sprites and on the stage.
  • Decide when a variable should be "For all sprites" or "For this sprite only".

Look at the corner of almost any game. Mario has a coin counter. Minecraft has a row of hearts. A racing game has a clock ticking down. Those numbers are how the game remembers what's happening, and without them it has no idea if you're winning or losing.

By the end of today's class, the corner of your stage will look like this:

And when that clock reaches 0, every sprite in your game will find out at the same moment, because one sprite will shout a message to all the others. Two new ideas make that work: variables and broadcasts.

#A variable is a box with a name on it

Picture a shoebox with score written on the lid. Inside is one number. Your scripts can peek inside, throw out the old number and put in a new one, or add a little to what's there. That box is a variable.

Variables live in the orange Variables category. To make one:

  1. Click Variables in the block list.
  2. Click Make a Variable.
  3. Type a name, like score.
  4. Choose For all sprites (more on this choice near the end).
  5. Click OK.

A round (score) block appears in the palette with a checkbox next to it. While that box is ticked, a little display called a monitor sits on the stage and shows the number live as your game runs.

💡 Tip

Right-click the monitor on the stage and pick large readout. You get just the number in a big orange box, which looks much more like a real game's scoreboard.

#Four blocks run every scoreboard

  • set empties the box and puts in a brand-new value. Whatever was there before is gone.
  • change adds to whatever is already in the box. To subtract, change by a negative number, like -1.
  • show variable and hide variable switch the monitor on and off from inside a script, handy for hiding the score on a title screen.

The round (score) block is a reporter: it reports what's in the box right now. Drop it into any round hole, like the one in say, and the sprite says the current score.

#Score: count up, but reset first

Here's the smallest game possible. Click the cat, earn a point, and watch it run away.

Click the cat three times and the monitor reads:

Now look at that first script. It does one boring, vital job: it puts the score back to 0 every time the green flag is clicked. Pull it off and play two games in a row, and your second game starts at 3 before you've clicked anything. Scratch remembers a variable's value until something changes it, even between games.

⚠️ Watch out

The number one variable bug is forgetting to reset. Every variable your game uses should get a set block right under when green flag clicked. If a game works the first time and acts strange the second time, look for a missing set.

#Lives: count down, then check for zero

Lives are a score running backward. You start with a few and lose one each time something bad happens. After every loss, you check whether any are left.

Why jump back to x: (-200) y: (0) right after losing a life? Scratch runs a forever loop about 30 times every second. If the diver stays on the shark, the very next pass sees it's still touching and takes another life, and the next pass takes another. Moving away from the danger means one bite costs exactly one life.

#Timers: two kinds of clock

#A countdown you build yourself

Make a variable called time left, then:

Each trip around the loop waits one second and knocks one off the clock, so the monitor counts 30, 29, 28, all the way down. When it reaches 0, the repeat until stops and the stage sends a message called time up that any sprite can react to. Messages get their own section below. Players can read this clock easily because it shows whole seconds.

#Scratch's built-in stopwatch

Scratch also has a stopwatch that is always running. It lives in the light-blue Sensing category.

reset timer puts the stopwatch back to 0, and (timer) reports how many seconds have gone by, with decimals, like 4.37. Use it for "how fast did you finish?" games, where you want to measure time instead of counting it down.

#Broadcast: one sprite tells everyone

Each sprite only knows about itself. But when a game ends, lots of things must happen at once: the player stops, the enemies vanish, and the stage shows a Game Over screen. How does everyone find out?

Think of the speaker system at school. The principal says "Fire drill!" once, and every classroom knows its own job: line up, grab the attendance sheet, close the door. The principal doesn't walk to each room. In Scratch, that announcement is a broadcast, and these blocks live in the yellow Events category:

To make a new message, click the little arrow on the broadcast block, choose New message, and type a name like game over.

Here is how that looks in blocks. The player notices its lives ran out and makes the announcement:

The stage hears it and changes the picture:

The enemy hears it and gets out of the way:

Notice what the player did not need to know: which backdrop to show, or how many enemies there are. It sent one message, and each listener handled its own job. Add a fourth sprite next week and you just give it a when I receive script; the player's code doesn't change at all.

#Broadcast and wait

There's a second version: broadcast (get ready v) and wait. It sends the message and then pauses the sending script until every script that received it has finished. Plain broadcast fires the message and keeps going immediately.

Use the waiting version when order matters, like a "3, 2, 1, Go!" countdown that must finish before the apples start falling:

The start message isn't sent until the countdown sprite has said all its numbers.

#For all sprites, or for this sprite only?

When you make a variable, Scratch asks you to choose.

  • For all sprites: one shared box that every sprite can read and change. Use it for score, lives, and time left, because many sprites need them.
  • For this sprite only: a private box that belongs to one sprite. Use it for something personal, like how fast one particular enemy swims.

If you make a variable while the Stage is selected, Scratch doesn't ask. Stage variables are always shared.

⚠️ Watch out

"I touch the coin and my score never changes!" Check this first: someone may have made score with For this sprite only, so there are two different boxes with the same name. A private variable's monitor shows the sprite's name in front, like Coin: score. If you see that, delete the private variable and make one shared score instead.

#Check your understanding

Use this script for the first question.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You click the green flag, then click the cat 3 times. What does the score monitor show?

  • The flag sets the box to 10, and each click takes away 2: 10, 8, 6, 4.

  • That's what you'd get if the score started at 0. The green flag script sets it to 10 first.

  • change by -2 subtracts. Only a positive number would add.

Show answer

A. The flag sets the box to 10, and each click takes away 2: 10, 8, 6, 4.

2These blocks run in order: set [score v] to (5), then change [score v] by (2), then change [score v] by (-1), then set [score v] to (10). What is score at the end?

  • That would be true if set added to the box. It doesn't; it replaces what's inside.

  • That's the value just before the last block runs. Then set throws the 6 away.

  • set empties the box and puts in 10, no matter what was there before.

Show answer

C. set empties the box and puts in 10, no matter what was there before.

3The player runs broadcast (gameover v). The enemy has a script under when I receive [game over v]. What does the enemy do?

  • Scratch doesn't guess. "gameover" and "game over" are two different messages.

  • The space makes them different messages. Pick the same message from the dropdown in both blocks.

  • Broadcasts arrive almost instantly, but only at scripts listening for that exact message.

Show answer

B. The space makes them different messages. Pick the same message from the dropdown in both blocks.

4A diver loses all 3 lives the instant it touches a shark. Which fix makes each bite cost exactly one life?

  • That makes the problem worse: one bite would still end the game.

  • Then lives reset to 3 every pass, so the diver could never lose.

  • The loop checks about 30 times a second. Once the diver isn't touching the shark, the next pass doesn't take another life.

Show answer

C. The loop checks about 30 times a second. Once the diver isn't touching the shark, the next pass doesn't take another life.

Key takeaways

  • A variable is a named box holding one value. set replaces it, change adds to it.
  • Reset every variable under when green flag clicked, or the second game starts where the first one ended.
  • After losing a life, move the player away from the danger, or the forever loop keeps counting the same hit.
  • broadcast lets one sprite announce an event; each sprite decides what to do under its own when I receive.
  • Use For all sprites for anything more than one sprite needs, like score and lives.

#Further reading

  • Variable (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): every variable block, plus local versus global variables, with pictures.
  • Broadcast (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): how messages travel, including clones and the order sprites hear them.
  • Timer (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): what the built-in stopwatch measures and when it resets.

What you'll learn

  • Use three shared variables (score, lives, time left) in one game.
  • Let the stage run the clock and reset the game.
  • End the game with one game over broadcast that every sprite answers.
  • Test every way a game can end, including playing a second time.

Apples are dropping out of the sky and you have one bowl. Catch an apple: +1 point and a happy pop. Miss one: lose a life. You have 30 seconds. When the clock runs out or your lives hit zero, the sky turns into a big GAME OVER sign and the bowl announces your final score.

Here is the finished game in numbers, partway through a round:

Every apple follows the same little loop, over and over, until the game ends:

Three sprites share the work. The Stage runs the clock and resets everything, the Bowl follows the arrow keys, and the Apple falls and keeps score. Build it step by step, and press the green flag after every step to see your progress.

#Step 1: Set up the sprites and backdrops

  1. Open a new project in Scratch.
  2. Delete the cat: right-click it in the sprite list and choose delete.
  3. Click Choose a Sprite and add Bowl. Then add Apple.
  4. Click Choose a Backdrop (bottom right) and add Blue Sky.
  5. Now paint a second backdrop. Hover over the backdrop button and pick Paint. Use the Text tool to write GAME OVER in big letters. In the name box at the top of the paint editor, rename this backdrop Game Over.

You should now have two sprites (Bowl and Apple) and backdrops named Blue Sky and Game Over.

💡 Tip

Scripts pick backdrops by name, so spell them the same way every time. A backdrop list with backdrop1, Game Over, and game over 2 in it is a bug waiting to happen. Delete the extras now.

#Step 2: Make the variables

Click Variables, then Make a Variable, three times. Choose For all sprites for each one:

  • score
  • lives
  • time left

Leave all three checkboxes ticked so their monitors appear on the stage. Drag the monitors into the top-left corner, out of the way of falling apples.

#Step 3: Steer the bowl

Click the Bowl sprite and build this:

Click the green flag. The bowl jumps to the bottom middle of the stage, and holding an arrow key slides it smoothly left or right.

There are two separate if blocks here, not one if/else. Each trip around the loop asks about both keys, and when you let go of both, nothing moves. Keep that in mind for the quiz at the end.

#Step 4: Let the stage run the clock

The stage is the best home for "whole game" jobs like resetting variables and counting down, because it never moves, hides, or gets deleted. Click the Stage (on the right, under the stage preview) and build this:

To make the game over message, click the arrow on the broadcast block, choose New message, and type game over.

Click the green flag and watch the monitors:

⚠️ Watch out

Don't skip switch backdrop to (Blue Sky v). When your first game ends, the stage is left showing the Game Over backdrop. This block brings the sky back when you play again.

#Step 5: Make the apple fall

Click the Apple sprite. This is the biggest script in the game, so build it slowly and read each block as you snap it in.

Here's what each part does:

  1. show makes sure the apple is visible. It hides at game over, so it has to come back for the next game.
  2. go to x: (pick random (-220) to (220)) y: (180) puts the apple at the top of the stage in a random spot.
  3. The repeat until loop moves it down 5 steps at a time and stops the moment the apple lands in the bowl or falls below it.
  4. The if/else asks why the loop stopped. Touching the bowl? Add a point and pop. Not touching? The apple was missed, so take a life.
  5. If that miss used up the last life, tell everyone with broadcast (game over v).
  6. The forever loop sends the apple back to the top for another drop.

If Pop isn't in the apple's sound list, open the Sounds tab, click Choose a Sound, and add it.

Play a round. Catch two apples and miss one:

#Step 6: Everyone answers "game over"

Right now the message gets sent and nobody is listening. Let's give every part of the game a job when it arrives.

On the Stage, add:

On the Apple, add:

On the Bowl, add:

stop [other scripts in sprite v] is the important block here. It freezes that sprite's forever loop, so the apple stops falling and the bowl stops sliding. On the stage, stop [other scripts in stage v] halts the clock, so a game you lost on lives doesn't keep ticking. The green join block (in Operators) glues words and a number together into one sentence.

Let the timer run out:

The sky changes to GAME OVER, the apple disappears, and the bowl says "Final score: 7" (or whatever you scored).

#Step 7: Test both endings, then test again

Good game designers test every way a game can end, plus the moment right after.

  • Clock ending: play and catch everything. At 0 seconds, the Game Over screen should appear.
  • Lives ending: click the green flag and don't touch the keys. After three misses the game should end, even with time left on the clock.
  • Play again: click the green flag a second time. Score should read 0, lives 3, time 30, the sky should be back, and the apple should be visible.

If a test fails, look for a missing set, show, or switch backdrop under a green flag first. That's where most second-game bugs hide.

#The finished scripts

Check your project against these. Each block below is everything on one sprite.

The Apple's two scripts are exactly the ones from Steps 5 and 6.

#Check your understanding

A classmate rewrote the bowl's loop like this:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The player clicks the green flag and doesn't press any keys. What does the rewritten bowl do?

  • It would with two separate if blocks. Here, "no key" means the else runs on every pass.

  • When left isn't pressed, the else branch runs, so the bowl moves right 8 steps every pass.

  • Left only moves the bowl while the left arrow is held down.

Show answer

B. When left isn't pressed, the else branch runs, so the bowl moves right 8 steps every pass.

2Why does the Apple's green-flag script begin with show?

  • Library sprites start visible. The trouble comes from the game itself.

  • Anything a game changes, like hiding a sprite, has to be undone when the green flag starts a new game.

  • show only makes a sprite visible; speed comes from change y by (-5).

Show answer

B. Anything a game changes, like hiding a sprite, has to be undone when the green flag starts a new game.

3You lose your last life with 10 seconds left on the clock. Which block stops the stage from later broadcasting game over a second time?

  • It halts the stage's countdown loop, so the clock never reaches 0 and never sends the message again.

  • That only stops the Apple's own scripts. The countdown lives on the Stage.

  • Hiding the apple doesn't affect the stage's clock at all.

Show answer

A. It halts the stage's countdown loop, so the clock never reaches 0 and never sends the message again.

Key takeaways

  • The stage is a good home for jobs that belong to the whole game: resetting variables and running the clock.
  • One game over broadcast can end the game for everyone, and each sprite decides how to react.
  • repeat until <<A> or <B>> stops when either thing happens; an if/else right after tells you which one it was.
  • Test both endings, and always test a second game. That's where missing resets show up.

#Make it yours

Pick one or two:

  • Speed it up. Make apples fall faster as your score grows: replace change y by (-5) with change y by ((-5) - ((score) / (5))).
  • Add danger. Add a second falling sprite, like a rock, that takes a life when you catch it.
  • Celebrate. Add a sprite that listens for game over, says "Nice try!", and does a little dance with turn right (15) degrees.

Save your project with File > Save to your computer or the Save now option if you're signed in. You'll use Apple Catcher again in Week 6.

#Further reading

  • Broadcast () block (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): exactly when a broadcast starts the scripts that hear it.
  • Stop () block (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): the difference between "all", "this script", and "other scripts in sprite".
  • Stage Monitor (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): normal readout, large readout, and slider, and how to move them.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create, reset, and change variables without looking at the notes.
  • Measure time with the built-in timer and glue words and numbers together with join.
  • Make sprites take turns with broadcast () and wait.
  • Track down a broadcast bug and add features to Apple Catcher.

Six exercises, getting harder as you go, then a challenge. Start each one in a new project unless it says to open your Apple Catcher. Give every exercise a real try before you open the hint, and try the hint before you open the solution. Being stuck for a few minutes is normal; that's the part where you're actually learning.

Three habits for this whole page:

  • Make every variable For all sprites unless the exercise says otherwise.
  • Every variable gets a set under when green flag clicked, unless the exercise tells you to keep its value.
  • Test by clicking the green flag at least twice. Bugs love the second game.

#Warm-up: predict the box

Without building anything, read this script and decide what the monitor shows after you click the green flag and press space twice. Then build it and check.

The flag puts 0 in the box, then adds 5. Each space press takes one away: 5, 4, 3.

#Exercise 1: Click counter

Make a variable called clicks. Every time you click the cat, clicks goes up by 1. When the green flag is clicked, clicks goes back to 0. Show the monitor on the stage.

After five clicks you should see:

Need a hint?

You need two scripts with two different hat blocks: one for the green flag, and one that runs when the sprite is clicked. Look in Events for the second one.

Show solution

Click the cat five times and the monitor shows clicks 5. Click the green flag and it drops back to clicks 0. The set handles the reset, and change does the counting.

#Exercise 2: Speed clicker

Now race the clock. When the green flag is clicked, the built-in timer resets. When clicks reaches 10, the cat says how many seconds it took, rounded to a whole number. Reuse your clicks scripts from Exercise 1.

If you click ten times in about four seconds, the cat says:

Need a hint?

Three blocks do most of the work: reset timer and (timer) from Sensing, and (round ()) from Operators. To make the cat wait for the tenth click, look for a Control block that pauses until something becomes true.

Show solution

wait until holds the script still until the tenth click. The two join blocks are nested so you can glue three pieces together: words, a number, more words. Look closely at the space inside [You took ] and at the start of [ seconds!]. Without them the cat says You took4seconds!.

#Exercise 3: Knock-knock joke

Add a second sprite (any animal). The two sprites tell a knock-knock joke, and each one must wait for the other to finish talking before it speaks. Use broadcast () and wait.

You should see one speech bubble at a time:

Need a hint?

The cat runs the whole joke from one green-flag script. Whenever it's the friend's turn, the cat sends a message and waits. The friend needs one when I receive script per line it says, so you'll make two messages.

Show solution

Now swap broadcast (who v) and wait for plain broadcast (who v) and run it again. The cat and the friend talk over each other, because plain broadcast doesn't pause the cat. The "and wait" is what turns two sprites into a conversation.

#Exercise 4: Spot the bug

A student put these two scripts on the Apple sprite. When lives hit 0, nothing happens and the apple keeps falling forever. Find the bug before you open the hint.

Need a hint?

Read the message name in the broadcast block, letter by letter. Then read the one in when I receive.

Show solution

The message names don't match. The script sends gameover (no space), but the receiver listens for game over (with a space). To Scratch those are two separate messages, and nobody is listening for gameover.

Fix it by choosing the same message from the dropdown in both blocks:

Both scripts are on the Apple, so when the message arrives, stop [other scripts in sprite v] also halts the forever loop that sent it. To keep this bug from coming back, make each message once and then always pick it from the dropdown, instead of typing a new message with almost the same name.

#Exercise 5: High score

Open your Apple Catcher. Add a variable called high score. When the game ends, if your score beats the high score, save it and have the bowl say "New high score!". Don't reset high score under the green flag; it should remember your best game.

Play once and score 6, then play again and score 9:

Need a hint?

The check belongs in the Bowl's when I receive [game over v] script. Compare (score) with (high score) using the > block, and only then use set.

Show solution

Replace the Bowl's when I receive [game over v] script with this:

After your 9-point game the bowl says "New high score!" and then "Final score: 9". Play a third time and score 4, and high score stays at 9, because 4 isn't bigger. A brand-new variable starts at 0, so your very first game always sets a record.

#Exercise 6: Bonus lives

In Apple Catcher, give the player an extra life each time the score reaches a multiple of 10 (10, 20, 30, and so on).

Catch your tenth apple and the monitors show:

Need a hint?

The (() mod ()) block in Operators gives the remainder after dividing. 20 mod 10 is 0, and 23 mod 10 is 3. Which scores give a remainder of 0 when you divide by 10?

Show solution

Find the "caught it" part of the Apple's script and add the inner if:

The new check sits after change [score v] by (1), so it looks at the score that includes this catch. Put it before, and the bonus arrives one apple late.

#Challenge: 3, 2, 1, Go!

Add a countdown to Apple Catcher before the apples start falling. Paint a new sprite called Countdown (a simple circle is fine). It says 3, 2, 1, Go! and then hides. Only after "Go!" should the clock start and the apples fall.

This is the trickiest one on the page because four parts of the game have to take turns. Here's the order they need to go in:

Need a hint?

The stage uses broadcast (countdown v) and wait, then sends a start message. On the Bowl and the Apple, the scripts that move things should begin with when I receive [start v] instead of when green flag clicked. The apple also needs to stay hidden during the countdown.

Show solution

On the Stage, change the green flag script so it waits for the countdown:

On the Countdown sprite:

On the Apple, drag when green flag clicked off the top of the falling script and put when I receive [start v] there instead. Do the same for the Bowl's movement script. Then give the Apple one new script so it isn't hanging in the sky during the countdown:

The game now pauses for about 3.5 seconds of countdown, then the apple appears and the clock starts at 30. The falling script already begins with show, so the apple pops into view right on "Go!".

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Make clones with create clone of, control them with when I start as a clone, and remove them with delete this clone.
  • Predict what a clone copies from its parent, including hidden sprites and private variables.
  • Avoid the two classic clone bugs: invisible clones and clones that multiply.
  • Build a My Block with an input, and explain why it makes scripts easier to fix.

Click the green flag and thirty snowflakes drift down a night sky, each from a different spot. How many snowflake sprites are in the sprite list? One. That single sprite makes copies of itself while the game is running, and each copy falls on its own and then disappears.

You could build the snowstorm the slow way: thirty sprites, each with the same script pasted in. Then you'd decide the flakes should fall a little faster, and you'd have to fix thirty scripts. Today you learn two ways out of that kind of trap: clones, which are copies of a sprite made while the game runs, and My Blocks, which let you invent your own blocks.

#A clone is a copy made while the game runs

A clone looks like its sprite and runs that sprite's clone scripts. When its job is done, it removes itself. You write the scripts once, and every clone uses them.

Three orange Control blocks do all the work:

  • create clone of (myself v) makes a new copy. The dropdown can also name a different sprite, to clone that sprite instead.
  • when I start as a clone is a hat block that only clones run. The original sprite never runs the script under it.
  • delete this clone removes the clone that runs it. If the original sprite runs it, nothing happens, so you can't delete your sprite by accident.

#A snowstorm from two scripts

Paint a small white circle and name the sprite Snowflake. Pick a dark backdrop so you can see it.

Click the green flag. Thirty flakes drift down, one every 0.2 seconds, each starting from its own spot along the top.

Here's who does what:

  1. The original Snowflake hides. Think of it as a hidden factory whose only job is making clones.
  2. The repeat (30) loop makes 30 clones, one every 0.2 seconds.
  3. Each clone runs when I start as a clone by itself: it picks a spot, shows itself, falls, and deletes itself at the bottom.

⚠️ Watch out

A clone starts as an exact copy of its parent, including being hidden. Because our factory hides itself, every clone is born hidden. Forget show in the clone script and your clones exist, fall, and delete themselves, all invisibly. If nothing appears on screen, check for show first.

#What a clone copies from its parent

At the moment it's born, a clone copies its parent's position, direction, costume, size, graphic effects, and whether it's showing. That's why each snowflake starts wherever the factory is standing, and why the clone script moves it to the top right away.

A clone also gets its own copy of any variable made For this sprite only, and from then on its copy is separate from everyone else's. Make a speed variable, choose For this sprite only, and try this clone script:

Now some flakes float and others zoom. Each clone picked its own speed and remembers it. ((0) - (speed)) turns a speed of 4 into -4, so the flake moves down.

A For all sprites variable works differently: there's only one box, and every clone shares it. That's exactly what you want for score, and exactly what you don't want for each flake's speed.

#Clones hear messages and keys too

Clones run every hat block in their sprite except when green flag clicked. That includes when I receive, when this sprite clicked, and when [space v] key pressed. Often that's handy: a single when I receive [game over v] script with delete this clone under it clears every clone at once.

Sometimes it's a nasty surprise:

Press space once and you get one clone. But now there are two copies of the sprite listening for space. Press again and both make a clone: four. Then eight. Then sixteen. The fix is to put the key script on a sprite that never gets cloned, like the player or the stage, and have it run create clone of (Laser v). You'll do exactly that in the code-along.

#The 300-clone limit

Scratch lets a project have up to 300 clones at once. After that, create clone of quietly does nothing. Clones that never delete themselves pile up until new ones stop appearing, so give every clone a way to end with delete this clone.

Clicking the green flag or the red stop sign removes every clone, so each game starts clean.

#My Blocks: invent your own block

Sometimes the same handful of blocks shows up in three or four places. My Blocks, the pink category at the bottom of the block list, lets you bundle them under a new name.

#Making a block with an input

  1. Click My Blocks, then Make a Block.
  2. Type a name, like jump.
  3. Click Add an input number or text, and name the input height.
  4. Click OK.

A pink define hat appears in your code area. Whatever you snap under it is what your new block does:

Now use it like any other block:

Space gives a small hop and the up arrow gives a big leap. Both run the same define script; only the height changes. The first loop rises in ten small steps so you can see the motion, and the second comes back down by the same amount.

#Why bother?

  • Shorter scripts. jump (60) is easier to read than eight blocks of arithmetic.
  • Fix it once. If the jump looks too slow, change the define script and every jump in the sprite is fixed.
  • Names explain your code. A script that says reset player tells you what it does without reading every block inside.

#A block with no inputs

Inputs are optional. This one puts a player back at the start:

Call reset player when the green flag is clicked, when the player loses a life, and when a new level begins. Three places, one definition.

#Four things that trip people up

  • My Blocks belong to one sprite. A block made in the Cat doesn't appear in the Dog. To share it, drag the define script onto the Dog in the sprite list, and Scratch copies it over.
  • Inputs only work inside their own define script. Drag the (height) reporter out of the define hat, not from Variables, and don't expect it to mean anything in other scripts.
  • To change a block, right-click its define hat and choose Edit.
  • Run without screen refresh is a checkbox in the Make a Block window. It makes the block finish in an instant without drawing each step. Leave it off for movement like jump, or the sprite teleports up and back and you never see the hop.

#Clones and My Blocks together

The two ideas team up nicely. Here's a block that makes a whole batch of clones:

In the Make a Block window, type spawn, add an input named count, then click Add a label and type flakes. Now spawn (10) flakes reads almost like a sentence.

#Check your understanding

Use this script for the first question.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You click the green flag. How many stars can you see on the stage?

  • Three clones exist, but look at what each one copied from its parent.

  • The original is hidden, and the clones are too.

  • The original hides before cloning, so every clone is born hidden, and nothing ever runs show.

Show answer

C. The original hides before cloning, so every clone is born hidden, and nothing ever runs show.

2A sprite has only when [space v] key pressed with create clone of (myself v) under it. You press space 3 times. How many copies of the sprite exist now, counting the original?

  • That would be right if only the original made clones. Every clone also listens for space.

  • The count doubles with each press: 2, then 4, then 8, because every copy makes a clone.

  • The original isn't a clone, but it still counts, and the clones make clones too.

Show answer

B. The count doubles with each press: 2, then 4, then 8, because every copy makes a clone.

3Eight fish clones each run set [speed v] to (pick random (1) to (6)), but speed was made For all sprites. What happens?

  • A shared variable is one box. Each new clone overwrites it for everyone.

  • Only For this sprite only variables give every clone its own copy.

  • Scratch never shows errors for this. The fish just don't behave the way you meant.

Show answer

A. A shared variable is one box. Each new clone overwrites it for everyone.

4You made a jump (height) block in the Cat. You click the Dog sprite and open My Blocks. What do you see?

  • My Blocks aren't shared between sprites automatically.

  • Each sprite has its own My Blocks. Dragging the define script to the Dog copies it.

  • Nothing red appears; the Dog simply doesn't have that block.

Show answer

B. Each sprite has its own My Blocks. Dragging the define script to the Dog copies it.

Key takeaways

  • A hidden "factory" sprite plus a when I start as a clone script can fill the stage with copies.
  • Clones copy everything about their parent, including being hidden, so the clone script usually needs show.
  • Every clone should end with delete this clone, or you'll hit the 300-clone limit.
  • Clones respond to keys and messages too. Put key scripts that make clones on a sprite that is never cloned.
  • A My Block bundles repeated code under one name: shorter scripts, and one place to fix.

#Further reading

  • Cloning (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): the three clone blocks, common uses, and how private variables work in clones.
  • My Blocks (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): every option in the Make a Block window.
  • Run Without Screen Refresh (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): what that checkbox really does and when to tick it.

What you'll learn

  • Fire projectiles by cloning a different sprite from the one that listens for the key.
  • Use a hidden "factory" sprite to make waves of enemy clones.
  • Write two My Blocks, explode and spawn wave (count), and call them from clone scripts.
  • Make each wave harder by using a variable in the movement math.

Your rocket is the last line of defense. Space rocks are raining down in waves: 3 rocks, then 6, then 9, each wave falling faster than the one before. Blast them with lasers before one of them hits you.

When it's working, the monitors tell the story of a good run:

Behind the scenes there are only three sprites. Every laser and every rock on screen is a clone, and two My Blocks keep the rock scripts short enough to read. Here's the loop the whole game runs on:

#Step 1: Set up the sprites and variables

  1. Start a new project and delete the cat.
  2. Add the Stars backdrop.
  3. Add the Rocketship sprite. In its Sounds tab, add the Laser1 sound.
  4. Add the Rocks sprite. In its Sounds tab, add Pop.
  5. Paint a new sprite: a short, thin, bright rectangle, about as tall as your finger is wide. Name it Laser.

Then make three variables, all For all sprites: score, wave, and rocks left. Keep all three monitors showing for now. You'll hide rocks left at the end, but while you build, it's the best way to see what the game is thinking.

#Step 2: Fly the rocket

Click Rocketship and build this:

Click the green flag. The rocket shrinks, parks at the bottom of the stage, and glides left and right with the arrow keys.

#Step 3: Fire laser clones

Still on Rocketship, add a second script:

Look at the dropdown: it says Laser, not myself. The rocket is never cloned, so exactly one copy of this script is listening, and each press makes exactly one laser. If the Laser sprite listened for space itself, every laser on screen would make another laser, and the count would double on every press.

Now click the Laser sprite and add:

Press space a few times. Lasers shoot up out of the rocket and vanish at the top of the stage.

⚠️ Watch out

Why the tiny wait (0.05) seconds? When a laser hits a rock, both sprites need to notice. If the laser deleted itself instantly, the rock might check a split second later and find nothing there. The short pause gives the rock time to see the hit.

#Step 4: A My Block that blows up rocks

Click Rocks. Before building the clone script, make a helper block.

  1. Go to My Blocks and click Make a Block.
  2. Name it explode. Don't add any inputs. Click OK.

Every hit rock does four things: adds a point, counts itself as gone, pops, and disappears. Bundling them into explode means the clone script only needs one block for all of it, and if you later want a bigger reward for each rock, there's exactly one place to change.

#Step 5: What each rock clone does

Still on Rocks:

Three things to notice:

  • change y by ((-1) - (wave)) speeds up each wave. In wave 1 a rock falls 2 steps at a time, in wave 2 it falls 3, in wave 3 it falls 4.
  • A rock that slips past you still counts itself as gone with change [rocks left v] by (-1) before deleting. Without that line, the wave could never end.
  • Touching the rocket sends game over. Make that new message from the broadcast dropdown.

You can't test this step on its own yet, because nothing creates rock clones. That's the next step.

#Step 6: A My Block that spawns a wave

Make one more block on Rocks. Click Make a Block, type spawn wave, click Add an input number or text, name it count, and click OK.

It fills in the counter first, then makes the rocks one at a time.

Now the main game loop, also on Rocks:

The original Rocks sprite hides and becomes the rock factory. Clones copy their parent's size, so setting the factory to 60% makes every rock 60% too.

Read the forever loop out loud and it sounds like a story: make a wave, wait until it's cleared, move on to the next wave, take a breath, repeat. Click the green flag and play. Wave 1 has 3 rocks, wave 2 has 6, wave 3 has 9.

#Step 7: Game over

When a rock hits the rocket, everything should stop.

On Rocks:

Every rock clone hears the message, freezes, and deletes itself. The original Rocks sprite hears it too. It can't delete itself, because delete this clone does nothing on an original, but stop [other scripts in sprite v] still halts its forever loop, so no new waves appear.

On Rocketship:

Let a rock hit you. The rocks vanish and the rocket says:

Two seconds later, stop [all v] ends the whole project.

#Step 8: Test like a game designer

Run through this list, and fix anything that fails before moving on:

  • Shoot every rock in wave 1. Does wave change to 2 after a one-second break?
  • Let one rock fall past you. Does rocks left still go down by one?
  • Hold the space bar. Do lasers come out at a steady rate, not in huge bunches?
  • Click the green flag after game over. Do score and wave reset?

When everything works, untick the rocks left checkbox so players don't see it.

#The finished scripts

Rocketship has the three scripts from Steps 2, 3, and 7, and Laser has the two from Step 3. Rocks has the most, so here they all are together:

#Check your understanding

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the space-key script live on the Rocketship, cloning Laser, instead of on the Laser sprite cloning myself?

  • Any sprite can use when [space v] key pressed.

  • Clones run key scripts. The rocket is never cloned, so it makes exactly one laser per press.

  • It works under any hat block. The problem is who else is listening.

Show answer

B. Clones run key scripts. The rocket is never cloned, so it makes exactly one laser per press.

2You delete the line change [rocks left v] by (-1) that comes after the falling loop. A rock slips past you. What happens?

  • Nothing sends it back; it still reaches delete this clone.

  • The opposite: the factory is waiting for rocks left to reach 0.

  • wait until <(rocks left) = (0)> waits forever for a rock that already left without counting itself.

Show answer

C. wait until <(rocks left) = (0)> waits forever for a rock that already left without counting itself.

3In wave 4, how many rocks does spawn wave ((wave) * (3)) make, and how many steps does each fall per move?

  • 4 × 3 = 12 rocks, and (-1) - (4) is -5.

  • That's adding 3 instead of multiplying, and it forgets the extra -1.

  • The count is right, but (-1) - (wave) gives -5 when the wave is 4.

Show answer

A. 4 × 3 = 12 rocks, and (-1) - (4) is -5.

Key takeaways

  • Put the key script that fires projectiles on a sprite that's never cloned, and clone the projectile sprite from there.
  • A hidden factory sprite sets things like size before cloning, and every clone inherits them.
  • Counting what's left (rocks left) lets the game know when a wave is over, but only if every way out of the wave counts down.
  • My Blocks such as explode and spawn wave (count) turn long clone scripts into a few readable lines.

#Make it yours

  • Survive longer. Add a lives variable so the rocket survives three hits before game over.
  • Mix up the rocks. Paint a second rock costume, then give each clone a random look with switch costume to (pick random (1) to (2)) in its clone script.
  • Shield up. Write a define shield block on the Rocketship that flashes it with change [ghost v] effect by (50) and back again.

#Further reading

  • Shooting Projectiles (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): other ways to fire bullets, including shooting in the direction a sprite faces.
  • When I Start as a Clone block (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): exactly what a new clone runs and when.
  • Custom Blocks (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): more examples of define scripts with inputs and labels.
