What you'll learn

  • Place clones exactly where you want them and remove them when they're done.
  • Give each clone its own private value with a For this sprite only variable.
  • Build My Blocks with one input, two inputs, and a label.
  • Explain and fix the "clones that multiply" bug.

These go from warm-up to "whoa." Each one is small, so start a fresh project every time and use any sprite you like unless the exercise names one. Try each exercise first, then the hint, and only then the solution.

💡 Tip

If your clones don't appear, check two things. Did the clone script run show? And did something actually run create clone of? Clicking a when I start as a clone script by itself does nothing, because only a brand-new clone starts that script.

#Warm-up: count the cats

Read this script and guess how many cats you'll see after the green flag, then build it to check.

The original is showing, so both clones are born showing too, but all three are standing on exactly the same spot. Put change x by (100) inside the loop, right after create clone of, and run it again. Now the cats spread out and you can count all three.

#Exercise 1: A row of five

Make the sprite put five copies of itself in a straight line across the middle of the stage, then hide the original. Use repeat, create clone of (myself v), and change x by.

You should see five sprites at x = -160, -80, 0, 80, and 160.

Need a hint?

A clone is born wherever its parent is standing at that moment. So the parent can walk along the line, dropping a clone at each stop. Where should the parent start, and how far should it move between clones?

Show solution

The parent drops a clone, steps 80 to the right, and repeats. That first show matters more than it looks: without it, the second time you click the green flag the parent is still hidden from last time, so every clone is born hidden too.

#Exercise 2: Pop the balloons

Add the Balloon1 sprite. Make 10 balloon clones in random spots. Clicking a balloon pops it (deletes the clone) and adds 1 to a popped variable.

Click all ten and you should see:

Need a hint?

You need three scripts: one that makes the clones, one that tells each new clone where to go, and one for clicks. Clones run when this sprite clicked too.

Show solution

The original hides, and hidden sprites can't be clicked, so only the clones respond. That's why the popped count can never go past 10.

#Exercise 3: A pulse block

Make a My Block called pulse with one number input named times. It makes the sprite grow by 20, wait 0.1 seconds, shrink back, and wait again, as many times as times says. When the sprite is clicked, it pulses 3 times.

Click the sprite and it should throb three times, then end at its normal size.

Need a hint?

Click Make a Block, type pulse, then Add an input number or text and name it times. Inside the define script, a repeat loop can use (times) as its count. Drag that (times) reporter out of the define hat.

Show solution

Each pass grows and shrinks by the same 20, so the sprite always ends where it started. Change the call to pulse (10) and it becomes a heartbeat.

#Exercise 4: Two inputs and a label

Make a block that reads hop (3) times height (40). It jumps up by height, waits 0.2 seconds, comes back down, waits again, and repeats times times. Space gives three small hops, and the up arrow gives one big one.

Need a hint?

In the Make a Block window, type hop, add an input named times, click Add a label and type times height, then add a second input named height. To come back down, you need the negative of height. What's 0 minus 40?

Show solution

((0) - (height)) turns 40 into -40, so each hop lands exactly where it took off. The label between the inputs is what makes the block read like a sentence.

#Exercise 5: Fix the firework bug

This Star sprite should launch one firework each time you press space. Instead, the first press makes 1, the next makes 2, then 4, then 8. Explain why, then fix it.

After the fix, pressing space five times launches exactly five fireworks.

Need a hint?

Which hat blocks does a clone run? Count how many copies of the Star are listening for the space key after each press, including the ones still in the air.

Show solution

Clones run when [space v] key pressed too. Every star still flying across the screen also makes a clone when you press space, so the number doubles each time.

Move the key script to something that's never cloned: the Stage. Delete the space-key script from the Star, then click the Stage and add:

Now only the stage listens for space, and each press makes exactly one star. The stage can't be cloned, so it's a safe home for any key script that makes clones.

#Exercise 6: A fish tank

Add the Fish sprite. Make 8 fish clones. Each fish swims at its own random speed between 1 and 6 and bounces off the edges, always facing the way it swims.

You should see eight fish going back and forth, some lazy and some zooming.

Need a hint?

Make a speed variable with For this sprite only, so each clone gets its own copy. Each clone sets its speed once, at birth. For facing the right way, look at set rotation style in Motion.

Show solution

Because speed is For this sprite only, every clone keeps its own value. Try making it For all sprites instead and all eight fish swim exactly alike, since there's only one shared box and the last clone born decides its value.

#Challenge: Number your clones

Make 5 clones in a row. Each clone gets its own number from 1 to 5. Clicking a clone makes it say which one it is:

This trick shows up in a lot of bigger Scratch games, any time the code needs to tell one clone from another, like knowing which enemy is the boss. Here's the idea in a picture:

Need a hint?

Make a my id variable For this sprite only. A clone copies its parent's private variables at the moment it's born, so the parent should change my id right before each create clone of. Each clone can then use its own my id to work out its x position.

Show solution

The clones line up at x = -160, -80, 0, 80, and 160, because clone 1 goes to 80 - 240, clone 2 goes to 160 - 240, and so on. Click the middle one and it says "I am clone number 3". The parent's own my id ends at 5, but that doesn't matter, because each clone took a snapshot of the value at birth.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a whole game's levels with one level variable and one start level message.
  • Give every game a clear way to win and a clear way to lose.
  • Run a playtest without helping, and turn what you see into a fix.
  • Track down the most common Scratch bugs, and share or remix a project the safe, fair way.

Your little brother plays your space shooter for twenty seconds. The rocks stop falling, nothing happens, and he turns to you: "Wait... did I win?"

That question means the game isn't finished yet. Every game that feels complete has three things: a goal to reach, a way to lose, and a challenge that grows as you get better. Then it needs to be tested by someone who isn't you, and fixed. Finally, if you want, it gets shared. This week covers all of it.

Here's the map of a small but complete game. Your Maze Escape in the code-along will look exactly like this:

Every arrow is something your code has to make happen, and every box is a screen the player should recognize.

#Levels: one variable, one message

A level is a stage of the game with its own layout or difficulty. Most Scratch games keep track of it with one variable, level, and one message that tells every sprite to get ready.

Every sprite listens for start level and sets itself up for whichever level it is. The stage, for example, picks the right backdrop:

To move up a level, change the variable and send the message again:

That's the whole pattern. To add Level 3 later, each sprite gets one more check in its start level script, and nothing else in the game has to change.

#Make later levels harder with math

New backdrops are nice, but you don't always need them. Put the level number into your movement math and the game gets harder by itself:

Level 1 falls 2 steps at a time, level 2 falls 4, level 3 falls 6. One block, as many levels as you like.

Other quick ways to raise the difficulty:

  • Less time on the clock.
  • More clones per wave.
  • Smaller targets, with set size to.
  • A new obstacle that only appears when level is greater than 1.

#Endings: no one should have to ask "did I win?"

A good ending has three parts:

  1. A check, like if <(lives) = (0)> or if <(level) > (2)>.
  2. A message, like broadcast (game over v) or broadcast (you win v).
  3. A screen: a backdrop, a sound, or a sprite that says clearly what happened.

You can also start scripts from the backdrop itself, with this hat block from Events:

💡 Tip

Test your endings first, not last. Temporarily set [lives v] to (1) so you can lose fast, or start at the final level so you can win fast. Then write yourself a note to change it back before you share.

#Playtesting: watch someone else play

Playtesting means watching another person play your game. It's the quickest way to find out what's confusing, because you already know how your game works and can't see it with fresh eyes anymore.

How to run a good playtest:

  1. Give the player your instructions, then stay quiet. Don't explain. If they're confused, that confusion is exactly what you came to find.
  2. Watch their hands and face. Where do they get stuck? Where do they grin?
  3. Write down what actually happens, not what you wish had happened.
  4. Afterward, ask three questions: What was the most fun part? What was confusing? Was it too easy, too hard, or about right?

Real playtest notes are short and specific:

#Debugging: think like a detective

A bug is anything your game does that you didn't mean it to. Every coder writes bugs, including the people who made Scratch. The skill isn't avoiding them; it's finding them.

#Detective tricks

  • Make it happen again. Find the exact steps that cause the bug: "When I touch the wall on Level 2, the score resets." A bug you can repeat is a bug you can fix.
  • Watch your variables. Tick the checkbox next to a variable so its monitor shows on the stage, and watch it change as you play.
  • Make sprites talk. Drop in a say block to show what a sprite "thinks" at that moment (there's an example right after this list).
  • Click one script. Clicking a script runs just that script, and it glows yellow while it runs. If it never stops glowing, it's stuck in a loop.
  • Slow it down. Put a wait (0.5) seconds inside a loop to watch each step, and take it out when you're done.

Here's the talking trick. Snap this into a loop and the sprite reports its lives every time around:

#The usual suspects

Most Scratch bugs are one of these:

What you see Likely cause
Works the first time, broken the second A variable or backdrop isn't reset under the green flag
A sprite is missing It hid last game and nothing tells it to show
A message does nothing The sender and receiver picked different message names
Score changes for one sprite but not another The variable was made For this sprite only
All lives vanish in one hit Still touching the enemy, so the loop counts the hit again and again
Clones stop appearing They never delete this clone, so you hit the 300 limit

Change one thing at a time, then test again. If you change five things and the bug disappears, you won't know which change fixed it, or which one quietly broke something else.

#Sharing and remixing the right way

When your game is ready, you can share it on the Scratch website so anyone can play. That needs a Scratch account, so check with a parent or guardian first.

#Before you click Share

On your project page, fill in two boxes:

  • Instructions: which keys to press, what the goal is, and how to win.
  • Notes and Credits: who made what. If you used someone else's art, music, or code, name them here.

#The Scratch Community Guidelines

Scratch is a community of millions of young people, and its guidelines come down to six ideas:

  • Treat everyone with respect, in projects and in comments.
  • Keep personal and contact information private. No real last names, addresses, phone numbers, school names, email addresses, or links to social media. Your username is all anyone needs.
  • Give helpful feedback. Say something you liked, then suggest an idea kindly.
  • Embrace remix culture. Building on others' work is welcome, as long as you give credit and make a meaningful change.
  • Be honest. Don't pretend to be someone else, and don't pass off someone else's project as your own.
  • Help keep the site friendly. If you see something mean or unsafe, click Report instead of arguing back.

#Remixing well

The Remix button on any shared project makes your own copy to change, and Scratch automatically adds a credit linking back to the original. To be a great remixer:

  • Change something real: new levels, new art, a new rule.
  • Say what you changed and thank the original creator in Notes and Credits.
  • Never remove someone's credit from a project you remixed.

#Not sharing online?

That's completely fine. Use File > Save to your computer to download your game as an .sb3 file. You can open it again later with File > Load from your computer, or send the file to your instructor.

#Check your understanding

A student added a Level 3 backdrop, but didn't change the stage's script:

Check your understanding

4 questions

1level is now 3, and start level is broadcast. Which backdrop appears?

  • Nothing in this script ever mentions Level 3, so Scratch can't pick it.

  • The else catches every level that isn't 1, including 3. Add a check for (level) = (3) to fix it.

  • The else branch always runs when level isn't 1.

Show answer

B. The else catches every level that isn't 1, including 3. Add a check for (level) = (3) to fix it.

2Your game works perfectly the first time. On the second green flag, the player is invisible. Which suspect do you check first?

  • A name mismatch would break the first game too.

  • The player hid at the end of the first game, and nothing makes it visible again.

  • Clicking the green flag removes every clone, so the limit resets each game.

Show answer

B. The player hid at the end of the first game, and nothing makes it visible again.

3During a playtest, your tester keeps pressing W to shoot and looks confused. What should you do right then?

  • Then you'll never learn what a stranger would do with your game.

  • That confusion is the most useful thing the playtest can show you. Fix the instructions afterward.

  • Let it play out; there may be more to learn in the next minute.

Show answer

B. That confusion is the most useful thing the playtest can show you. Fix the instructions afterward.

4Which line is safe to put in your project's Notes and Credits?

  • It gives credit and says what changed, with no personal information.

  • A school name is personal information that the guidelines ask you to keep private.

  • Email addresses are contact information. Keep conversations in Scratch comments instead.

Show answer

A. It gives credit and says what changed, with no personal information.

Key takeaways

  • One level variable plus one start level message can run every level of a game.
  • Every ending needs a check, a message, and a screen the player can't miss.
  • During a playtest, watch and take notes. Don't explain.
  • Debug by making the bug happen again, watching variables, and changing one thing at a time.
  • Share with a grown-up's OK, give credit, make meaningful changes when you remix, and keep personal information off Scratch.

What you'll learn

  • Run two levels from one level variable and one start level message.
  • Keep the player out of the walls with a My Block that has two inputs.
  • Use broadcast () and wait so the game doesn't skip ahead before sprites are ready.
  • Build both a win ending and a lose ending, and playtest every path through the game.

You're a tiny green dot trapped in a maze. Reach the gold star to escape to Level 2. Touch the red lava and you're sent back to the start of the level, minus one life. Lose all three lives and it's game over. Escape both levels and you win.

In Week 3 you built a maze with solid walls. This one is a full game: it has levels, a way to lose, a way to win, and My Blocks that keep the code tidy. Here's every path a player can take through it:

By the end of Step 8, you'll have tested every arrow in that picture.

#Step 1: Paint the backdrops

You'll paint four backdrops. Click the Stage, open the Backdrops tab, and use the paint editor.

  1. Level 1: Draw maze walls with the rectangle tool in one color, like dark blue. Add two or three small red rectangles as lava. Leave open space in the bottom-left corner (the start) and the top-right corner (the goal).
  2. Level 2: Right-click Level 1 in the backdrop list and choose duplicate, then rename the copy. Make it harder: narrower paths and more lava. This time leave space in the top-left (start) and bottom-right (goal).
  3. You Win: Write YOU ESCAPED! with the text tool.
  4. Game Over: Write GAME OVER.

Name them exactly Level 1, Level 2, You Win, and Game Over, and delete the blank backdrop1.

⚠️ Watch out

Use exactly the same wall color everywhere, and don't use that blue or the lava red anywhere else, including on your sprites. The game decides what counts as a wall by color alone, so a blue eye on your player would make it stick to itself.

#Step 2: Add the sprites and variables

  1. Delete the cat.
  2. Paint a new sprite: a small green circle. Name it Player.
  3. Add the Star sprite from the library. Rename it Goal and set its size to about 50.

Make two variables, both For all sprites: level and lives.

#Step 3: A My Block that respects walls

Here's the wall trick from Week 3, packed into one reusable block: move a little, and if that move put you inside a wall, move straight back. It happens between screen refreshes, so the player never appears inside the wall.

On Player, click Make a Block. Type try move x, add a number input called dx, add a label y, add a number input called dy, and click OK.

To set the color in touching color, click the color circle, choose the eyedropper at the bottom, and click a wall on the stage. Your color code will look different from the one above, and that's fine.

In Week 3 you wrote the undo four times, once per arrow key. Now it's written once, and each arrow just says which way to try.

#Step 4: A My Block for losing a life

Still on Player, make a block called lose a life with no inputs. Add the Zoop sound to Player first.

If you still have lives, start level sends you back to the start of the level you're on. Nothing about the level changes, only your position.

#Step 5: Everyone gets ready for each level

Each part of the game listens for start level and checks which level it is.

On the Stage:

On Player:

On Goal:

If a start or goal spot lands inside one of your walls, drag the sprite to an open spot on the stage and copy its x and y from the sprite info panel into the script.

#Step 6: The main game loop

On Player:

Use the eyedropper again to set the lava color.

Look how readable this is. Four try move blocks handle the walls, lose a life handles lava, and the goal check handles levels. The My Blocks hide the fiddly parts.

Why broadcast (start level v) and wait instead of plain broadcast? It pauses this loop until the player has actually moved to the new start. Without the wait, the loop could check touching (Goal v)? once more before the player moves, still be on the star, and jump straight past Level 2.

Play it now and watch the monitors:

On the Stage:

On Goal:

On Player:

stop [other scripts in sprite v] freezes the Player's main loop, so the arrow keys stop working on the ending screens.

#Step 8: Playtest every path

Go back to the diagram at the top and test each arrow:

  • Walk into every wall. Can you slip through anywhere? If so, make that wall thicker.
  • Touch lava. Do you go back to the start of the same level with one fewer life?
  • Touch lava three times. Do you see Game Over?
  • Beat both levels. Do you see You Win?
  • Click the green flag after each ending. Is the player visible, back on Level 1, with 3 lives?

Then hand the game to someone else and watch them play without helping. Write down one thing that confused them.

💡 Tip

To test Level 2 quickly, temporarily change set [level v] to (1) to set [level v] to (2). Change it back before you share.

#Check your understanding

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The player is pressed right up against a wall on its right side, and you hold the right arrow. What does try move x (3) y (0) do?

  • It does move 3 steps, but then it notices the wall color and moves back.

  • The undo uses (0) - (dx), which is -3, cancelling the move before the screen redraws.

  • Only lava sends you to the start, through lose a life.

Show answer

B. The undo uses (0) - (dx), which is -3, cancelling the move before the screen redraws.

2You reach the star on Level 1. Why does the goal check use broadcast (start level v) and wait instead of plain broadcast?

  • It works anywhere. The difference is whether this loop pauses.

  • Waiting means the player is already at the new start when the loop carries on.

  • The backdrop changes at the same speed either way.

Show answer

B. Waiting means the player is already at the new start when the loop carries on.

3What would happen if you deleted the else branch from lose a life, keeping only the if <(lives) = (0)> part?

  • Nothing sends the player back to the start, so each pass of the loop sees lava again and calls lose a life again.

  • The loop only sends start level when you reach the goal.

  • The player is still touching lava on the next pass, about a thirtieth of a second later.

Show answer

A. Nothing sends the player back to the start, so each pass of the loop sees lava again and calls lose a life again.

Key takeaways

  • One level variable and one start level message set up every sprite for each level, and resend the player to the start after a mistake.
  • A My Block with inputs, like try move x () y (), turns four copies of the wall trick into one.
  • Use broadcast () and wait when the next step depends on sprites finishing their setup first.
  • Test every arrow in your game's map, including clicking the green flag after each ending.

#Make it yours

  • Race the clock. Add a 60-second limit with reset timer and if <(timer) > (60)> then in the Player's loop.
  • Level 3. Paint a third backdrop, give each start level script a check for (level) = (3), and change the win check to <(level) > (3)>.
  • A guard. Add an enemy that glides back and forth across a corridor. In the Player's loop, add if <touching (Enemy v)?> then with lose a life inside.

  • Broadcast () and Wait block (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): exactly what the waiting version waits for.

What you'll learn

  • Add a level that rises with the score and makes the game harder.
  • Give a game a winning ending that can't clash with its losing ending.
  • Find bugs by reading scripts and watching variables, then fix one thing at a time.
  • Decide what belongs on a shared project page and what stays private.

This set has three flavors. Exercises 1 and 2 add levels and a way to win to your Apple Catcher from Week 4. Exercises 3 to 5 are bug hunts: read the script, work out what's wrong, and fix it. Exercise 6 is about sharing. Before you change Apple Catcher, save a copy with File > Save to your computer so you can always go back.

For the bug hunts, use the detective's loop from the notes:

#Warm-up: which suspect?

Each of these is one of the "usual suspects" from the notes. Name the cause before reading the answer underneath.

#Exercise 1: Level up every 5 points

In Apple Catcher, add a level variable that starts at 1. Each time the score reaches a multiple of 5, the level goes up by 1, and the apple falls faster on higher levels.

After catching 10 apples, the monitors should read:

Need a hint?

You used mod for bonus lives in Week 4; the same trick works here with 5. For the speed, put (level) into the number in change y by, so a higher level means a bigger step down.

Show solution

On the Stage, add set [level v] to (1) next to the other set blocks in the green flag script.

On the Apple, change the falling block and the "caught it" branch:

On level 1 the apple falls 5 steps at a time, on level 2 it falls 7, and on level 3 it falls 9. Scores 5 and 10 each bump the level, which is how 10 catches gets you to level 3.

#Exercise 2: A way to win

Right now Apple Catcher can only end badly. Add a winning ending: catch 20 apples and the game shows a You Win backdrop and stops. Paint the backdrop first.

When you catch apple number 20, the sky should switch to your You Win backdrop and stay there, even if the clock had time left.

Need a hint?

The Apple knows the moment the score changes, so the check goes there and sends a new message. The stage answers it, but think about what the stage's countdown loop might do after you've already won.

Show solution

On the Apple, inside the "caught it" branch, right after change [score v] by (1):

On the Stage:

stop [other scripts in stage v] stops the countdown, so the clock can't reach 0 and broadcast game over after you've already won. Two endings fighting over the screen is a classic bug, and this one block prevents it.

#Exercise 3: Bug hunt, the instant game over

This player has 3 lives, but a single touch of the ghost takes all of them. Why? Fix it so each touch costs exactly one life.

Need a hint?

Tick the lives checkbox and play slowly. How many times does the forever loop run while the player is still overlapping the ghost? What could make the script hold still until they're apart?

Show solution

The forever loop runs about 30 times a second. While the player is still touching the ghost, every pass takes another life, so three passes later you're at 0.

One fix is to wait until they're no longer touching:

Now each touch costs exactly one life. Sending the player back to the start, the way Maze Escape does, works too.

#Exercise 4: Bug hunt, the broken second game

The first game works. But on the second green-flag click, the player is invisible and the game starts on Level 2. Find the two missing blocks.

Need a hint?

List everything that changes during a game: position, lives, level, and whether the player is showing. Now check which of those the green flag script puts back.

Show solution

The sprite hides at game over and nothing shows it again. And level is never reset, so it keeps last game's value.

Rule of thumb: anything that can change during a game must be put back under when green flag clicked.

#Exercise 5: Bug hunt, double points

In this catching game, catching an apple sometimes adds 2 points instead of 1. Here are the scripts from two sprites:

Need a hint?

Both scripts sit inside forever loops. Scratch gives each sprite a turn, one after another, many times a second. What happens if the Bowl gets its turn while the apple is still sitting in it?

Show solution

Both sprites notice the same catch, and both add a point. If the Bowl's loop gets its turn before the Apple moves back to the top, it sees the touch too. Whether it does depends on which sprite Scratch runs first, which is why the bug only shows up sometimes.

Pick one sprite to own the score. The Apple is the better choice, because it also moves itself away right after. Delete the if block from the Bowl, and every catch adds exactly one point.

When two sprites both react to one event, you often get double results. One job, one owner.

#Exercise 6: A safe, honest project page

Write the Instructions and Notes and Credits for your Maze Escape. Then decide which of these five lines are OK to include:

Need a hint?

Go back to the Community Guidelines section of the notes. Which lines would help a stranger find or contact Maya outside of Scratch?

Show solution

OK: A, C, and D.

Not OK: B and E. A school name and an email address are personal and contact information, and the Scratch Community Guidelines ask you to keep those private. Your Scratch username is all anyone needs.

A good page might look like this:

#Challenge: Best time

In Maze Escape, record how fast the player escapes. Start the stopwatch when the game begins. When the player wins, save the time in a best time variable, but only if it beats the old record or there's no record yet. Show the result in a speech bubble.

Escape in 41 seconds, then in 35, and the second win shows:

Need a hint?

Put reset timer just before the Player's forever loop. On a win, compare (timer) with (best time). A brand-new variable holds 0, so "no record yet" means best time is 0. You'll need an or to check both cases.

Show solution

On Player, add reset timer to the green flag script, right before the forever loop.

Then replace the Player's win script:

Don't reset best time under the green flag, or it forgets your record every game. The <(best time) = (0)> half of the or is what lets the very first win count as a record.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain every requirement in the capstone brief and where you learned it.
  • Choose a game idea that's small enough to finish and big enough to meet the brief.
  • Write a one-sentence pitch and check it against every requirement.
  • Sketch a storyboard and list the sprites, backdrops, variables, and messages you'll need.

For six weeks you've built games someone else designed: a catching game, a space shooter, a maze. Now you're the designer. You decide who the player is, what they're trying to do, and what's standing in their way.

Before anyone builds anything, real game studios spend days planning on paper, because changing a sketch takes seconds and changing a finished game takes hours. Today you'll plan. Here's the whole capstone at a glance:

This lesson is the first column. The next lesson builds the game one milestone at a time, and the last one tests, polishes, and presents it.

#The brief

Make an original game in Scratch 3. It can be about anything you like, as long as it's kind and appropriate for everyone. Your game must include all of these:

Requirement What it means Where you learned it
Instructions The player knows how to play: on a title screen, in a speech bubble, or on the project page Week 6
Score or timer A variable the player can see that counts points or time Week 4
Collisions Something happens when sprites touch each other, a color, or the edge Week 3
A clone At least one sprite makes copies of itself or of another sprite Week 5
A My Block At least one block you defined yourself and actually use Week 5
Two levels At least two levels that look or play differently Week 6
Win and lose A clear winning ending and a clear losing ending Week 6

#What you turn in

  1. Your game: a shared Scratch link, or your .sb3 file from File > Save to your computer.
  2. Playtest notes: what happened when at least one other person played your game.
  3. One fix: a short write-up of one thing you changed because of playtesting.

Your instructor will tell you the due date and how to send your file or link.

#Pick an idea

Here are six ideas that fit the brief, sorted from the most manageable to the most ambitious. Borrow one, mash two together, or invent your own.

Starter-sized (great if this is your first game from scratch):

  • Bug Catcher. Bugs crawl across a garden (clones). Click them for points before the timer runs out. Level 2 adds fast bugs and a bee you must not click.
  • Snowball Fight. Targets pop up around the stage (clones). Throw snowball clones at them. Hit 10 to reach Level 2, where the targets move.

Medium:

  • Meteor Dodge. Meteors fall (clones) and you steer a ship to dodge them. Survive 20 seconds to reach Level 2, where meteors fall faster. The next lesson builds this one as its example.
  • Pizza Rush. Toppings fall from the sky. Catch the good ones and dodge the burnt ones. Level 2 adds a topping that's worth double.

Ambitious (pick one only if you finished last week's projects with time to spare):

  • Deep Sea Diver. Swim around collecting pearls while sharks patrol. Level 2 is deeper and darker, with more sharks and less air on a timer.
  • Ghost House. A maze with ghosts gliding back and forth. Find the key to open the door to Level 2.

💡 Tip

Choose the smaller idea. A simple game that works and feels finished beats a giant game that's half built. Once the basics work, you can always add more.

#Step 1: Write your pitch

A pitch is one or two sentences that tell someone what your game is. If you can't say it simply, the idea might be too big.

A good pitch names the player's goal (click bugs), the danger (the bee), and the pressure (time runs out). Read yours out loud. Would a friend know what to do in the first five seconds?

#Step 2: Check your idea against the brief

Go down the brief's table and write how your game will meet each row. Here's the check for Bug Catcher:

If any row is empty, change your idea until every row has an answer. An empty row now is a missing requirement later.

#Step 3: Draw a storyboard

A storyboard is a set of quick sketches, like a comic strip, showing each screen of your game. Grab a sheet of paper and fold it into six boxes. Draw one screen in each:

Stick figures and boxes are perfect, and nobody is grading the drawing. Draw arrows to show which way things move, and label every sprite.

#Step 4: List what you'll build

Before you open Scratch, write down everything you'll need. This list becomes your checklist while building, and it catches problems early, like a sprite that needs a variable nobody made.

#Step 5: Build your first script today

Most games start the same way: show a title screen, wait for the player, then start Level 1. You can build this right now, before anything else. Put it on the Stage:

Paint a backdrop called Title with your game's name and "Press SPACE to start." Click the green flag. The title appears, and nothing happens until you press space. Then the start level message goes out, ready for your sprites to listen for.

This one script already covers two parts of the brief: instructions, and resetting your variables for every new game.

#Check your plan with a buddy

Before you build, show your pitch and storyboard to a classmate, a family member, or your instructor. Ask them:

  • Does this game sound fun?
  • Is anything confusing?
  • Does it look small enough to finish?

Change your plan if you need to. Erasing a box on paper takes 30 seconds.

#Your planning checklist

  • A one- or two-sentence pitch.
  • Every row of the brief has an answer.
  • A six-box storyboard.
  • A list of sprites, backdrops, variables, and messages.
  • The title-screen script works.
  • Someone else has seen your plan.

#Further reading

  • Scratch Ideas (opens in a new tab): official tutorials and coding cards, handy when you need one specific trick for your game.
  • Game (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): the kinds of games Scratchers make most often, with tips for each.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Break a game into milestones that each end with something you can play.
  • Start from a skeleton: backdrops, sprites, variables, and a stage script that runs the levels.
  • Add a player, clones, and collisions, using a My Block in each.
  • Finish with win and lose endings that stop everything cleanly, then check every requirement.

Nobody builds a LEGO castle by dumping out every brick and hoping. You build the base, check that it holds, add a wall, check again. Games get built the same way, one milestone at a time. After each milestone your game should run without breaking, even though it isn't finished yet.

Every milestone below uses an example game called Meteor Dodge: steer a ship, dodge falling meteors, and survive 20 seconds on each of two levels. Your game will be different, but each milestone works the same way. Use these scripts as a starting point and change them to fit your idea.

💡 Tip

After each milestone, use File > Save to your computer and put the milestone number in the file name, like meteor-dodge-m2.sb3. If you break something later, you can load the last good version and lose only one milestone of work.

#Milestone 1: The skeleton

Set everything up before writing any game code:

  • Backdrops: a painted Title (game name plus how to play), Level 1, Level 2, You Win, and Game Over. For Meteor Dodge, add Stars and one more space backdrop from the library and rename them Level 1 and Level 2.
  • Sprites: add them all now, even if they don't do anything yet. Meteor Dodge has Ship and Meteor.
  • Variables: lives, level, and time left, all For all sprites.

Then put the game's "boss" script on the Stage. It shows the title, resets the variables, and runs each level's clock:

Read the big loop from the top: fill the clock, announce the level, count down, move to the next level, and stop once you're past Level 2. Notice that set [time left v] to (20) comes before broadcast (start level v), so any sprite that hears the message can trust the clock is already full.

Done when: the title shows, space starts Level 1, the clock counts down, Level 2 appears at 0, and after Level 2 the backdrop stops changing.

#Milestone 2: The player

Make the player move, and give it a My Block for getting back to the start. On Ship:

The ship hides on the title screen and appears when a level starts. When Level 2 begins, the stage sends start level again, and Scratch restarts this script from the top, so the ship snaps back to the start for the new level.

Done when: the ship shows up on Level 1, moves left and right, and returns to the middle when Level 2 starts.

#Milestone 3: Clones and collisions

Now the danger. On Meteor, make a My Block that drops one meteor, and a factory loop that keeps calling it:

On Level 1 the factory makes a meteor every second and each falls 3 steps at a time. On Level 2 it makes one every half second and they fall 6 steps at a time. Both changes come from the level variable, with no extra code.

⚠️ Watch out

Why does the start level script begin with delete this clone? Clones hear messages too. Without that block, every meteor still falling when Level 2 starts would run the forever loop and start making meteors of its own. The first block deletes those leftover clones. The original isn't a clone, so it skips past delete this clone and keeps spawning. Bonus: Level 2 starts with an empty sky.

Next, add the collision to the Ship. Put this if inside the Ship's forever loop, under the two arrow-key checks. Add the Zoop sound to Ship first.

The wait (1) seconds gives the player a moment to recover, so a single meteor can't take two lives.

Done when: meteors fall faster and more often on Level 2, and getting hit lowers lives by exactly 1.

#Milestone 4: Win and lose endings

Every sprite needs to react to both endings.

On the Stage:

On Meteor, one script for each message:

On Ship:

The stage's stop [other scripts in stage v] matters most here. It stops the level clock, so a game you've already lost can't suddenly jump to Level 2 when the timer runs out.

Done when: losing all your lives shows Game Over with no meteors still falling, and surviving both levels shows You Win.

#Milestone 5: Instructions and juice

"Juice" is game-designer slang for the small touches that make a game feel alive. Add a few:

  • A sound when the level changes.
  • A say [Level 2!] for (1) seconds on the Ship at the start of Level 2.
  • A costume change or change [color v] effect by (25) when the player gets hit.
  • Background music. On the Stage's Sounds tab, add a sound from the Loops category, then put play sound () until done inside a forever loop in a when I receive [start level v] script.

Make sure your Title backdrop says exactly how to play: which keys, what the goal is, and how to win.

Done when: someone who has never seen your game can read the title screen and start playing without asking you anything.

#Check your requirements

Meteor Dodge now covers every row of the brief:

Make the same list for your own game. Anything missing goes into your next milestone.

#When you get stuck

  • Load your last saved milestone and add one piece at a time.
  • Check the usual suspects from Week 6: missing resets, hidden sprites, mismatched message names.
  • Tick the checkboxes for your variables and watch the monitors while you play.
  • Ask your instructor, and show them the exact steps that make the problem happen. "When I lose on Level 2, the ship comes back" is much easier to fix than "it's broken."

#Further reading

  • Define () block (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): how define scripts and their inputs work, for when your My Block misbehaves.
  • Global Variable (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): why lives and level must be shared by every sprite.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Try to break your own game with a self-test checklist.
  • Run a real playtest, take notes, and choose the one fix that matters most.
  • Write up a fix as problem, change, and result, then test it again.
  • Save or share your game safely, present it in about two minutes, and check it against the rubric.

Your game runs. Now comes the part that makes it good. "It works when I play it" is a long way from "it's fun for someone who has never seen it." The last stretch of any game project is testing, fixing, and showing it off. Game studios call it polish, and it's often what players remember most.

Here's the loop you'll go around at least once:

#Round 1: Try to break it yourself

Before anyone else plays, try your hardest to break your own game. Work through this list and fix anything that fails:

  • Both endings. Win once. Lose once. Does each one show the right screen and stop the game?
  • Play again. Click the green flag after each ending. Is every variable back to its starting value? Is every sprite visible and in the right place? Is the title or Level 1 backdrop showing?
  • Both levels. Does Level 2 really look or play differently?
  • Strange players. Mash every key. Hold an arrow key the whole time. Don't touch anything at all. Does the game still behave?
  • Clones. Play for a few minutes. Do clones keep appearing, or do they stop? Stopping is a sign they never get deleted.

💡 Tip

Testing a long game takes forever. Temporarily set time left to 5, or start on level 2, so you can reach the endings quickly. Write yourself a sticky note to change them back.

#Round 2: A real playtest

Find at least one person who hasn't played your game: a family member, a friend, or a classmate in a breakout room. Two testers are even better.

Use the playtest rules from Week 6:

  1. Let them read your instructions, and don't explain anything else.
  2. Watch quietly. Your job is to notice, not to help.
  3. Write down what they do and say.
  4. At the end, ask three questions: What was fun? What was confusing? Too easy, too hard, or just right?

Use this template for your notes. They're part of what you turn in.

#Pick your one fix

Your tester probably found several things. You need to make at least one fix and write it up. Pick the one that matters most, in this order:

  1. Broken: something doesn't work, like a sprite missing in the second game.
  2. Unfair or confusing: the player didn't know what to do, or lost for no good reason.
  3. Too easy or too hard: speeds, timers, or the number of clones.
  4. Looks and sounds: nice to have, but last.

#An example fix

In the notes above, the tester got hit the moment Level 2 began, because meteors start falling before the player is ready. That's "unfair," so it beats everything except a broken game. The fix: give the player a one-second head start before spawning begins.

#Polish checklist

With time left over, pick a few:

  • Sounds for scoring, getting hit, winning, and losing.
  • A "Level 2!" message so players notice the change.
  • A "Click the green flag to play again" line on your ending backdrops.
  • Tidy code: right-click an empty part of the code area and choose Clean up Blocks, then delete leftover test scripts.
  • Check that the monitors don't cover anything important.

#Save it or share it

To turn in a file: use File > Save to your computer. You'll get an .sb3 file. Give it a clear name, like meteor-dodge-final.sb3.

To share a link (only with a Scratch account and a grown-up's OK):

  1. Click Share in the editor.
  2. On the project page, fill in Instructions and Notes and Credits.
  3. In Notes and Credits, name anything you didn't make yourself. Library sprites are fine to use, but if you remixed a project or used someone's art or music, thank them by username.
  4. Check that nothing on the page, in your sprites, or on your backdrops shows your last name, school, location, or photos of you.
  5. Copy the link from your browser's address bar.

#Present your game

You'll have about two minutes to show your game to the class. Use this plan:

  1. Pitch (15 seconds): your one-sentence description.
  2. Demo (60 seconds): play a bit of Level 1, then show Level 2 and one ending.
  3. Code tour (20 seconds): show one script you're proud of, like your My Block or your clone script.
  4. Playtest fix (15 seconds): what your tester found and how you fixed it.
  5. Next time (10 seconds): one thing you'd add with another week.

⚠️ Watch out

Demos love to break when people are watching. Practice once beforehand, and keep a copy of your last working .sb3 file ready to open with File > Load from your computer, just in case.

#The rubric

Use this before you turn anything in. Every row in the middle column is required; the right column is how to go further.

Part Complete Extra polish
Instructions The player can learn the keys, goal, and how to win without asking you A title screen with a "Press SPACE to start" prompt
Score or timer A visible variable that changes as you play A high score or best time that survives between games
Collisions At least one touch (sprite, color, or edge) changes the game Different reactions to different things you touch
Clones At least one sprite uses clones, and they get deleted Clones with their own speed or ID
My Block At least one block is defined and used A My Block with an input that you call more than once
Two levels Level 2 looks or plays differently Difficulty uses level in the math, or there's a Level 3
Endings A clear win and a clear lose, and the green flag starts a fresh game Sounds or animations on each ending
Playtest Notes from at least one tester Two testers, or a second round after your fix
Fix write-up Problem, change, and whether it worked A before-and-after of the script
Good Scratcher Credit for anything you didn't make, and no personal information Instructions and Notes and Credits filled in on a shared page

#What comes next

Your game doesn't have to stop when the class does. Keep adding levels, ask a friend to remix it, or try one of the official tutorials on the Scratch Ideas page. When you're ready for something new, everything you learned here (variables, loops, if blocks, messages, and your own blocks) carries straight into text-based languages like Python, where the ideas are the same and only the typing is different.
